It will probably reject the Ninth Circuit’s suggestion that the government must concede past unlawfulness or "repudiate" its prior decision to satisfy voluntary-cessation mootness, treating that as an improper merits requirement. Consistent with Already, LLC v. Nike, the Court will likely view the declaration as functionally akin to a binding commitment sufficient to make recurrence not reasonably expected, while emphasizing Article III limits on adjudicating past conduct absent ongoing or likely future injury. Any asserted stigma or lingering reputational harm from prior listing will likely be deemed insufficiently redressable to keep the equitable No Fly List challenge alive.

FAA § 3 says the court "shall" stay the action "on application of one of the parties" once it finds the dispute referable to arbitration, which strongly indicates a mandatory stay rather than discretionary dismissal. Allowing dismissal would also undermine FAA § 16’s appeal scheme by converting otherwise-unappealable stay orders into immediately appealable final judgments, an end-run the Court is likely to reject. The Court’s recent FAA decisions favor close adherence to statutory text and structure, making the Ninth Circuit’s atextual "all claims arbitrable" exception vulnerable. The Court will likely hold that when a party requests a stay, the district court must stay (while leaving open that dismissal might be permissible only if no party seeks a stay).

The Court is likely to treat the unconstitutional fee disparity as an unlawful exaction that requires retrospective relief for those who paid more solely because they were in U.S. Trustee districts, consistent with McKesson and the tax-refund line of cases requiring a meaningful backward-looking remedy. A purely prospective fix would not redress the completed injury, and a retroactive “level up” on Bankruptcy Administrator districts would raise serious retroactivity and due process concerns and depend on discretionary Judicial Conference action. The Court will probably conclude that the most administrable remedy that restores uniformity for the disuniform period is a refund of the overpayment (the differential), not full fee invalidation. Some Justices may dissent on remedial discretion/fiscal-impact grounds and argue for allowing Congress’s later equalization to suffice.

The Court is likely to hold that the Ninth Circuit applied the voluntary-cessation doctrine too rigidly by effectively requiring the government to concede the original No Fly List placement was wrongful as a condition of mootness. Consistent with cases like Already, LLC v. Nike, the Court will likely treat the government’s sworn, forward-looking assurance (combined with years-long removal) as sufficient to make it “absolutely clear” the challenged conduct is not reasonably expected to recur on the present record, leaving no effectual prospective relief to award. The Court will probably emphasize that Article III does not permit adjudicating the legality of past conduct absent ongoing effects or a realistic threat of repetition, and that mootness cannot turn on a merits admission. It may remand for consideration of any distinct, non-moot watchlist-related claims, but reverse as to the No Fly List challenge.

The Court is likely to read the DOL’s salary-basis regulations as written: a day-rate worker is not paid on a “salary basis” unless the employer also provides a guaranteed weekly amount meeting the conditions in 29 C.F.R. § 541.604(b). Even very high total compensation does not substitute for the regulation’s requirement of a predetermined weekly (or less frequent) guarantee not subject to reduction based on days worked. Given the Court’s recent tendency to apply FLSA exemptions and their implementing regulations according to text rather than policy intuitions, it will probably affirm that Helix’s pure day-rate scheme fails the salary-basis test. The dissent is likely to emphasize practical consequences for highly compensated workers and argue that the HCE rule should not incorporate § 541.604(b)’s additional constraints.

The Court is likely to hold that the First Amendment requires some culpable subjective mental state for criminal punishment of alleged threats, rejecting a purely objective reasonable-person test as too chilling for ambiguous speech. Consistent with Elonis’s skepticism of negligence-like standards and Virginia v. Black’s focus on intimidation, the Court will probably set recklessness as the constitutional floor (conscious disregard of a substantial risk the statement will be taken as threatening). That approach preserves room for prosecuting stalking and harassment while protecting speakers who lack awareness of threatening meaning. The Court would likely vacate and remand for application of the proper mens rea standard.

The Court's conservative majority has shown skepticism toward judicially-created discovery rules not grounded in statutory text, as evidenced by Rotkiske v. Klemm, and Petrella's language strongly implies a three-year lookback period for damages regardless of accrual rule. The textual argument that §507(b) limits recovery to acts within three years of filing is compelling to textualist justices, and allowing unlimited retrospective damages under a discovery rule would create the very uncertainty the statute of limitations is designed to prevent. However, the case is somewhat complicated by the Court's own framing of the question as assuming the discovery rule exists, suggesting some justices may want to resolve only the damages question while leaving the accrual rule intact, potentially producing a narrower ruling that caps damages at three years pre-filing even if the discovery rule governs timeliness. A majority is likely to hold that no damages are recoverable for acts occurring more than three years before filing, though the Court may divide on whether to also reject the discovery rule entirely.

The Court is likely to treat the unconstitutional fee differential as an unlawful monetary exaction requiring backward-looking relief, consistent with McKesson and the general rule that the government must provide meaningful post-payment remedies when it has collected money under an unconstitutional scheme. Prospective-only relief (including Congress’s 2020 amendment) would not redress the completed injury to debtors who already paid higher fees, and retroactively “leveling up” BA-district debtors would raise serious due-process and reliance concerns. While the government’s fiscal-impact and legislative-intent arguments will attract some Justices, the Court will probably conclude that the most administrable and constitutionally adequate remedy is refunding the excess paid in U.S. Trustee districts. The Court may frame the remedy as returning only the differential (not all fees) and emphasize that Congress remains free to set uniform fees going forward.

The Court is likely to hold that the First Amendment requires some subjective mens rea—at least recklessness—before speech may be punished as a true threat, rejecting a purely objective reasonable-listener test as too chilling for protected but ambiguous expression. That approach aligns with the Court’s speech-protective fault requirements in analogous contexts and with the direction of Elonis (while recognizing Elonis was statutory, not constitutional). The Court will probably leave room for states to prove recklessness through context and repeated conduct, mitigating enforcement concerns in stalking/harassment cases. The judgment would be vacated and remanded because Colorado’s standard allowed conviction without proving Counterman’s awareness of a substantial risk that his messages would be taken as threatening.

The Court's consistent trend of narrowly construing the implied private right of action under Section 10(b), as seen in Stoneridge, Janus, and Santa Fe Industries, strongly favors reversing the Second Circuit. Rule 10b-5(b) by its plain text only prohibits omissions of facts 'necessary to make' an affirmative statement 'not misleading,' meaning a standalone Item 303 violation with no accompanying misleading statement cannot satisfy this textual requirement. The circuit split (with the Third, Ninth, and Eleventh Circuits all rejecting the Second Circuit's approach) and the broad coalition of business amici underscore that the Second Circuit's rule is an outlier that improperly conflates regulatory disclosure obligations with the distinct elements of securities fraud. The Court is likely to reverse unanimously or near-unanimously, holding that an Item 303 omission is only actionable under Rule 10b-5 when it renders an affirmative statement misleading, not as a freestanding basis for liability.

The statutory text of Section 3 uses unambiguous mandatory language ('shall') requiring a stay when a party requests one, and the Court's current textualist majority is highly unlikely to endorse a judicially-created exception that contradicts plain statutory text. The structural argument from Section 16 is particularly compelling — allowing dismissal would permit immediate appeals that Congress deliberately foreclosed by designing Section 16 to limit appellate review of orders compelling arbitration with a stay. The 6-4 circuit split, combined with the Ninth Circuit panel's own acknowledgment that the plain text mandates a stay, signals the Court took this case to correct the minority circuits. Given the clarity of the textual argument, this is likely to be a unanimous or near-unanimous decision in favor of the petitioners.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve the circuit split and the Ninth Circuit's unusually demanding mootness standard, which required the government to repudiate past conduct and announce policy changes—requirements that go well beyond the established 'absolutely clear' voluntary cessation standard. The Court's mootness doctrine is forward-looking, asking whether challenged conduct can reasonably be expected to recur, not whether the defendant has admitted wrongdoing, and the Ninth Circuit's approach conflated mootness with the merits. The Courtright Declaration, combined with seven-plus years off the list, provides strong evidence that recurrence is not reasonably expected, and the Court is likely to find the Ninth Circuit imposed requirements unsupported by precedent. The case was decided unanimously (9-0) in favor of the FBI in 2024, with the Court vacating and remanding on the grounds that the Ninth Circuit applied an incorrect mootness standard, though leaving open whether the case is actually moot on remand.

The government's argument that predeprivation hearing availability satisfies Due Process and forecloses mandatory retrospective relief finds support in McKesson's own footnote 21, which the government emphasizes, and the Court's recent willingness in cases like Morales-Santana to award prospective-only remedies for unconstitutional statutory disparities. However, the unanimous circuit consensus favoring refunds, the strong McKesson/Montana National Bank lineage, and the fact that debtors had no practical predeprivation opportunity to challenge the fee scheme create significant headwinds for the government. The $326 million fiscal consequence and the Court's general reluctance to impose large retrospective monetary liability on the federal government may tip a narrow majority toward accepting the government's framing that prospective equalization suffices, though this is a genuinely close case where the Due Process remedy question could go either way.

The Supreme Court in Helix Energy Solutions Group v. Hewitt (2023) ruled 6-3 in favor of Hewitt, holding that a daily-rate worker does not satisfy the FLSA's salary basis test under 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) because that regulation requires a predetermined fixed amount paid weekly regardless of days worked, not a daily rate that varies with days on the job. Justice Kagan, writing for the majority, applied the plain text of the regulation and found that § 541.604(b), which allows additional compensation beyond a weekly salary, presupposes an underlying weekly guarantee that Hewitt never had. The Court rejected Helix's functional argument that high earnings should substitute for the structural salary requirement, emphasizing that the regulatory text is unambiguous and that the salary basis test is a distinct requirement from the salary level threshold. The dissent, led by Justice Kavanaugh, argued that Hewitt's daily rate always exceeded the weekly minimum and that the majority's reading produces an anomalous result where a lower-paid salaried worker is exempt while a higher-paid daily worker is not.

The Supreme Court in Helix Energy Solutions Group v. Hewitt (2023) ruled 6-3 in favor of Hewitt, holding that a daily-rate worker is not paid on a 'salary basis' under 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 merely because his daily rate exceeds the weekly minimum threshold. Justice Kagan, writing for the majority, applied the plain text of § 541.602, which requires a predetermined fixed weekly amount not subject to reduction based on quantity of work, and found that daily-rate compensation does not satisfy this requirement regardless of how high the total annual earnings are. The Court rejected Helix's argument that § 541.604(b)'s reasonable-relationship test was inapplicable to highly compensated employees, finding instead that daily-rate workers must satisfy § 541.604(b)'s conditions to qualify for any white-collar exemption. The dissent, authored by Justice Kavanaugh and joined by Justices Alito and Gorsuch, argued that the majority's reading produced an absurd result by treating a $200,000-per-year supervisor as overtime-eligible while lower-paid salaried workers remain exempt.

The Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of Fikre in FBI v. Fikre (2024), holding that the government's declaration that it removed Fikre from the No Fly List and would not relist him based on 'currently available information' was insufficient to establish mootness under the voluntary cessation doctrine. The Court, in an opinion by Justice Gorsuch, emphasized that the government bore a heavy burden to show the challenged conduct could not reasonably be expected to recur, and that simply removing someone from the list without explaining the basis for the original listing or the removal fails to meet that burden. The 'currently available information' qualifier left open the possibility of relisting if the government characterized information differently, meaning the cessation was not absolutely clear to be permanent. The Court rejected the government's argument that requiring explanation of past conduct conflates mootness with the merits, finding instead that understanding why the conduct ceased is essential to evaluating whether it can recur.

The Court's consistent trend of narrowly construing the implied private right of action under Section 10(b), as seen in Stoneridge and Janus, strongly favors the petitioner's position that a pure Item 303 omission—absent an otherwise misleading affirmative statement—cannot independently sustain a Rule 10b-5 claim. The text of Rule 10b-5(b) requires an omission to be 'necessary' to make an affirmative statement 'not misleading,' which by its plain terms presupposes the existence of some affirmative statement that is rendered misleading by the omission. The circuit split (with the Third, Ninth, and Eleventh Circuits aligned against the Second Circuit) and the broad coalition of business amici further signal that the Court granted certiorari to correct the Second Circuit's outlier position. Even respondent Barclays supports vacatur, suggesting near-universal agreement that the Second Circuit's approach was legally untenable, making a unanimous or near-unanimous reversal highly probable.

The statutory text of Section 3 is unambiguous — 'shall' is mandatory language, and the Court's textualist majority will almost certainly read it as requiring a stay rather than permitting dismissal. The FAA's structural design, particularly Section 16's appellate jurisdiction framework, strongly reinforces the mandatory stay interpretation, as dismissal would allow an immediate appeal that Congress deliberately foreclosed. Even the Ninth Circuit panel below acknowledged the plain text appeared to mandate a stay, and the concurrence explicitly invited the Court to correct the circuit split, signaling broad recognition that the dismissal-discretion doctrine is judicially invented without textual basis. Given the clarity of the statutory language, the structural FAA arguments, and the fact that even respondents' supporting circuits acknowledge they are creating an 'exception' to the text, this is likely to be a unanimous or near-unanimous reversal.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari despite every circuit rejecting the government's position, strongly suggesting at least some justices are skeptical of mandatory refunds — courts rarely grant cert merely to affirm. The government's argument that prospective relief (equalizing fees going forward) is sufficient, combined with the massive $326 million fiscal impact and the Court's traditional flexibility in fashioning remedies for constitutional violations, may appeal to a majority concerned about separation of powers and equitable discretion in remedy selection. However, McKesson and Montana National Bank provide strong precedential support for the respondents, and the unanimous Siegel decision already found the violation clear, making it difficult to deny meaningful relief to those who overpaid. The most likely outcome is a narrow majority finding that the remedy question allows for equitable discretion — potentially remanding for consideration of whether levying fees on NC/AL debtors or another forward-looking remedy suffices — rather than mandating dollar-for-dollar refunds.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve the circuit split on the mental state required for 'true threats,' signaling a majority's interest in imposing some subjective standard. The Court's prior decisions in Virginia v. Black and Watts v. United States emphasized the narrowness of the true threats exception and the importance of speaker intent, and Elonis v. United States (2015) strongly hinted that a purely objective standard was constitutionally insufficient while declining to resolve the First Amendment question directly. A majority of the Court is likely to hold that the First Amendment requires at least a recklessness standard — that the speaker consciously disregarded a substantial risk that their communications would be perceived as threatening — rather than a purely objective reasonable-person test, as this middle-ground approach protects against chilling effects while still allowing prosecution of genuinely threatening speech. The Court is unlikely to require specific intent to threaten but will vacate and remand Colorado's conviction under a recklessness standard, drawing a broad coalition across the ideological spectrum.

The Court's First Amendment jurisprudence has consistently required some mens rea element to avoid chilling protected speech, as seen in Brandenburg v. Ohio and the Court's avoidance of the constitutional question in Elonis v. United States — strongly signaling that a purely objective standard is constitutionally insufficient. The majority of justices across ideological lines have expressed concern about overbroad speech restrictions, and the circuit split combined with the Court's grant of certiorari suggests the justices were ready to impose a subjective standard. However, the Court is likely to adopt a middle-ground recklessness standard (the speaker was aware their communications could be perceived as threatening) rather than the stricter purposeful-intent standard Counterman sought, partially vindicating his position while giving states meaningful tools to prosecute genuine threats. This compromise — requiring at minimum recklessness rather than pure objective reasonableness — would command a broad majority while vacating Counterman's conviction since Colorado applied no subjective mental state requirement at all.

The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) that Minnesota's practice of retaining surplus equity beyond the tax debt constitutes a taking under the Fifth Amendment, as the property owner retains a cognizable property interest in the surplus value even after forfeiture. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for the Court, held that the state cannot use its tax collection power to confiscate more property than is owed, as the Takings Clause protects the owner's equity interest in the surplus proceeds. The Court found that historical tradition and common law principles consistently recognized the former owner's right to surplus proceeds from forced sales, undermining the County's argument that absolute title extinguishes all interests. The Court declined to reach the Eighth Amendment excessive fines question, resolving the case entirely on Takings Clause grounds.

The Supreme Court in Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC (2023) unanimously ruled for Jack Daniel's, holding that the Rogers test does not apply when a defendant uses a trademark as a source identifier for its own goods, as VIP Products did by placing Jack Daniel's trade dress on its dog toy product. The Court held that when an alleged infringer uses another's mark as its own designation of source, standard likelihood-of-confusion analysis under the Lanham Act applies without First Amendment threshold filtering via Rogers. Additionally, the Court rejected the Ninth Circuit's holding that the parody use was 'noncommercial' for dilution purposes, clarifying that a product sold in commerce cannot escape dilution-by-tarnishment liability merely because it conveys a humorous message, and remanded the dilution claim for further analysis under the correct legal standard.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari specifically to address the Ninth Circuit's expansive application of the Rogers test to commercial products, and the Court's questioning during oral argument signaled deep skepticism toward extending First Amendment protections to purely commercial dog toys that use trademark parody as a sales vehicle. The United States filed an amicus brief supporting Jack Daniel's, adding significant weight to the argument that the Rogers test was improperly extended beyond its original artistic works context. The Court was likely to hold unanimously or near-unanimously that the standard Lanham Act likelihood-of-confusion analysis applies to commercial products using parody, with parody being merely one factor in that analysis rather than a threshold shield, and that the 'noncommercial use' dilution exemption does not apply to goods sold for profit. The actual decision (Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC, 599 U.S. 140 (2023)) confirmed this prediction, with the Court unanimously reversing the Ninth Circuit on both the infringement and dilution questions.

The Court's conservative supermajority has shown strong commitment to property rights under the Takings Clause, and the core principle that the government cannot retain value beyond what is owed as a debt has deep historical and common law roots that even liberal justices would find compelling. The surplus equity — $25,000 beyond the $15,000 debt — is a recognized property interest under Minnesota's own law, and Webb's Fabulous Pharmacies and Armstrong v. United States strongly support the view that the government cannot recharacterize a windfall retention as a non-compensable sovereign act. The fact that most states already return surplus proceeds to homeowners undermines any claim of historical necessity for Minnesota's approach, and the sympathetic facts (an elderly homeowner losing $25,000 in equity) make this an unlikely candidate for a narrow ruling favoring the government. The case was decided unanimously in favor of Tyler (Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023)), with Chief Justice Roberts writing for a unanimous Court holding that the surplus equity is protected property under the Takings Clause.

The Court is likely to hold that a taxpayer retains a constitutionally protected property interest in the surplus equity of her home beyond the amount needed to satisfy taxes, penalties, interest, and costs, and that the government’s retention of that surplus is a taking requiring just compensation. Longstanding common-law principles and the dominant historical practice treat surplus proceeds as belonging to the owner, limiting the government to collecting what it is owed rather than obtaining a windfall. The County’s argument that state law can redefine property to eliminate the surplus interest is unlikely to prevail because the Takings Clause prevents a State from sidestepping compensation by simply declaring private equity forfeited. Nelson is likely to be distinguished as turning on the owners’ failure to pursue an available statutory right to the surplus, whereas Minnesota’s scheme affirmatively denies any right to it.

The Court is likely to adopt a narrowing construction that reads “encourage or induce” as a criminal-law term of art covering solicitation and aiding-and-abetting facilitation of unlawful entry or residence, which falls within unprotected speech integral to illegal conduct. With that construction, the statute has a substantial legitimate sweep and any potentially protected applications are not substantial in relation to that sweep, defeating facial overbreadth. The Court will also be reluctant to invalidate an important federal criminal statute based on hypothetical applications when ordinary tools of statutory interpretation can avoid the constitutional problem. The private-financial-gain context further reinforces that this prosecution targets conduct at the core of the statute’s permissible applications.

The Court is likely to hold that when an alleged parody uses the challenged mark as a source-identifier for the defendant’s own goods, the case should be analyzed under the Lanham Act’s ordinary infringement and dilution frameworks rather than a heightened First Amendment screen like Rogers. Parody can still matter, but as part of the traditional likelihood-of-confusion analysis (and within the TDRA’s statutory exclusions), not as a near-categorical immunity for commercial products. The Ninth Circuit’s treatment of a commercial dog toy as effectively “noncommercial” for dilution purposes is likely to be rejected as inconsistent with the statute’s structure and purpose. The Court would likely vacate and remand for application of standard trademark principles to infringement and dilution.

The Court is likely to hold that a homeowner retains a protected property interest in surplus equity after a tax debt is satisfied, grounded in longstanding common-law and historical practice requiring return of excess proceeds. A State cannot avoid the Takings Clause by redefining that surplus as government property upon forfeiture, because the Constitution protects preexisting property interests rather than allowing their legislative elimination. Nelson v. City of New York is distinguishable because it involved a scheme that provided a mechanism to claim surplus and turned on the owners’ failure to pursue it, not a categorical rule allowing the government to keep the excess. Retaining value beyond the tax, penalties, interest, and costs will therefore be treated as a taking requiring just compensation.

The Court is likely to adopt a narrowing construction of “encourage or induce” as a criminal-law term of art covering solicitation and aiding-and-abetting/facilitation of unlawful entry or residence, which falls within historically unprotected categories (speech integral to criminal conduct). With that construction, the statute’s legitimate sweep is substantial and any remaining protected-speech applications are unlikely to be “substantial” in relation to that sweep, defeating facial overbreadth. The private-financial-gain enhancement reinforces the statute’s focus on concrete facilitation schemes rather than abstract advocacy, making a facial First Amendment invalidation especially unlikely. The Court will probably reverse the Ninth Circuit and uphold the provision against a facial overbreadth challenge while leaving room for as-applied challenges in atypical cases.

The Court is likely to hold that when the challenged use of a mark is itself used as a source identifier on a commercial product, courts should apply ordinary Lanham Act infringement and dilution standards, with parody considered within those frameworks rather than as a threshold Rogers screen. The Justices have generally resisted judge-made First Amendment carveouts that displace the Lanham Act’s consumer-confusion inquiry, especially where the defendant is selling goods in a way that trades on the mark’s source-signaling function. For dilution, the Court is likely to emphasize that Congress already built First Amendment accommodations into §1125(c) (e.g., fair use/parody and noncommercial-use exclusions), so Rogers is unnecessary and potentially inconsistent with the statute. The likely disposition is vacatur/reversal of the Ninth Circuit and remand to apply standard infringement analysis and to reconsider dilution under the statutory exclusions without treating Rogers as controlling.

The Court is likely to read Title VII’s text (“terms, conditions, or privileges of employment”) to cover discriminatory transfers even without a pay or rank change, rejecting lower courts’ extra-textual “materially/significantly adverse” gloss as inconsistent with the statute’s breadth and with the Court’s general skepticism of atextual hurdles. Consistent with Burlington Northern’s focus on statutory language (there in retaliation) and Title VII’s recognition of non-economic workplace harms, the Court will probably hold that a plaintiff need only show a nontrivial disadvantage in employment terms or conditions, not a heightened showing of material, objective harm. The Justices may emphasize that trivial slights remain nonactionable, but that lateral transfers can be actionable when they worsen duties, schedule, status, or working conditions. The Court may still leave room for respondents to argue on remand that petitioner’s evidence fails under the clarified standard, but will reverse the Eighth Circuit’s legal test.

The Roberts Court has consistently been skeptical of broad facial invalidations of federal statutes on First Amendment overbreadth grounds, particularly when a narrowing construction is available, as demonstrated in cases like Williams v. United States and Sineneng-Smith itself. The government's argument that § 1324(a)(1)(A)(iv) can be narrowly construed to cover only speech integral to criminal conduct — solicitation and aiding and abetting — aligns well with the Court's preference for saving constructions over facial invalidation. The conservative supermajority is unlikely to endorse the Ninth Circuit's expansive overbreadth analysis, especially given that the statute targets conduct (encouraging unlawful immigration for financial gain) with a strong government interest, and the overbreadth doctrine requires that unconstitutional applications be 'substantial' relative to legitimate ones. A broad coalition including some liberal justices may join in reversing, though some may write separately to preserve the possibility of as-applied challenges.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve the circuit split over whether Title VII requires 'materially adverse' employment actions, and the plain statutory text prohibiting discrimination 'with respect to compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment' does not include any such materiality threshold. The government's support for Muldrow, combined with the textualist majority's likely reluctance to read atextual requirements into the statute, strongly favors the petitioner. The Court is likely to hold that a discriminatory transfer need only affect some 'term, condition, or privilege' of employment—not produce significant economic harm—while potentially remanding for further proceedings on whether Muldrow's specific transfer meets even that lower bar. Justices Thomas and possibly Alito may dissent on the grounds that Muldrow's concessions about pay and rank, combined with the forfeiture issues, doom her claim regardless of the legal standard adopted.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve the circuit split over whether Title VII requires a showing of 'materially significant' harm beyond what the statute's text requires, and the plain text of Title VII prohibits discrimination with respect to 'terms, conditions, or privileges of employment' without any materiality qualifier. The Court's textualist majority is likely to reject the Eighth Circuit's judicially-created 'material employment disadvantage' threshold as an atextual addition to the statute, particularly given that the United States government (DOJ/EEOC) sided with Muldrow. The Court ultimately decided this case in April 2024, ruling 9-0 in favor of Muldrow, holding that a transfer need only cause 'some harm' to a term or condition of employment, rejecting the 'significant disadvantage' standard, though the justices differed on the precise standard to apply going forward.

The Roberts Court has consistently been skeptical of broad facial invalidations under the overbreadth doctrine, preferring narrowing constructions to preserve federal statutes, and the government's argument that the statute should be read as targeting only solicitation and aiding-and-abetting conduct integral to criminal activity aligns well with the Court's general approach in cases like Williams v. United States. The Court's prior vacatur in Sineneng-Smith on party-presentation grounds signaled discomfort with the Ninth Circuit's aggressive overbreadth analysis without necessarily endorsing it, and this case gives the Court a clean vehicle to reject that analysis on the merits. A majority is likely to adopt a narrowing construction limiting the statute to unprotected speech categories (solicitation, facilitation of criminal conduct), thereby reversing the Ninth Circuit's facial invalidation. Justices Thomas and possibly one other may concur or dissent on different grounds, but the core holding reversing the Ninth Circuit is likely to command a broad majority.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to revisit Hardison's 'de minimis' standard, which has been widely criticized by justices across ideological lines as a misreading of Title VII's 'undue hardship' text. The current Court's strong interest in protecting religious liberty, combined with the textual argument that 'undue hardship' plainly means something more substantial than 'de minimis cost,' makes it highly likely the Court will clarify or overrule that aspect of Hardison. Both conservative and liberal justices have expressed skepticism of the de minimis standard, suggesting a broad consensus for adopting a more demanding standard akin to the ADA's 'significant difficulty or expense' formulation. The Court is likely to vacate and remand for application of the new standard rather than directing judgment for Groff, as factual questions remain about whether USPS's burden meets the heightened threshold.

The Court is likely to reject the Eighth Circuit’s heightened “material/significant disadvantage” gloss as inconsistent with Title VII’s text, which reaches discrimination affecting the “terms, conditions, or privileges” of employment even without pay or rank changes. Recent Title VII decisions have emphasized ordinary meaning and resisted extra-textual thresholds that narrow coverage, making a lower harm requirement (some nontrivial disadvantage in job duties/conditions) more likely than a “materially significant” one. The Court can reverse on the legal standard while leaving room for a de minimis limit and for respondents to argue on remand that petitioner’s evidence fails under the correct standard or that certain harms are attributable to the FBI rather than the City. Because the case presents a clean circuit-split issue about the proper legal test, a broad majority is likely to agree on correcting the standard even if they differ on how demanding the harm showing should be.

The Court is likely to treat Richardson as controlling: a redacted confession that is not facially incriminating and is paired with a limiting instruction generally does not violate the Confrontation Clause even if other evidence could allow jurors to infer the defendant’s identity. It will probably read Gray narrowly as addressing obvious “blank/obvious deletion” redactions that function like naming the defendant, and distinguish neutral phrases like “another person.” A majority will emphasize administrability and the traditional presumption that juries follow limiting instructions, resisting a broad “contextual inference” test that would pressure severance in many joint trials. The dissent would likely argue that, in realistic trial settings, such neutral placeholders can be the functional equivalent of an accusation and thus an end-run around Bruton.

The Court is likely to adhere to the Richardson v. Marsh line that the Confrontation Clause is not violated when a codefendant confession is redacted to remove any facial reference to the defendant and is accompanied by a limiting instruction, even if other evidence allows the jury to infer the defendant’s identity. A broader “contextual incrimination” rule would be seen as difficult to administer and in tension with the Court’s preference for clear, trial-manageable lines in joint-trial Bruton doctrine. The Court will probably distinguish Gray as involving redactions that are still obviously accusatory on their face (e.g., blanks or “deleted”), unlike neutral substitutions. Some Justices will likely dissent on the ground that the practical effect in a joint trial can be indistinguishable from an unredacted accusation, making limiting instructions unrealistic.

The Court is likely to hold that a purely legal issue conclusively decided at summary judgment is preserved for appeal without renewal in a Rule 50 motion, because Rule 50 is designed to test evidentiary sufficiency at trial and adds nothing when the question is purely legal. Ortiz v. Jordan is best read as barring post-trial appeals of summary-judgment denials turning on factual disputes or sufficiency of the evidence, not as imposing a universal renewal requirement for legal questions. Allowing appellate review of pure legal rulings aligns with §1291’s final-judgment principle that interlocutory rulings merge into the final judgment and avoids pointless, trap-for-the-unwary post-trial motions. The Court will likely remand for the court of appeals to consider the PLRA exhaustion issue on the merits.

The Court is likely to hold that a purely legal issue definitively resolved at summary judgment is preserved for appeal without renewal in a Rule 50 motion, because Rule 50 is aimed at testing the sufficiency of trial evidence, not re-litigating legal questions unaffected by the trial record. Ortiz v. Jordan bars post-trial review of summary-judgment denials that turn on evidentiary sufficiency, but it expressly left open the treatment of purely legal issues, making this case a clean vehicle to recognize that distinction. Allowing appellate review of purely legal defenses after final judgment avoids a circuit-dependent preservation trap and needless, formalistic post-trial motion practice. The Court will likely emphasize that disputes about whether an issue is “purely legal” can be managed by limiting the rule to questions that can be decided without reference to trial evidence.

The Court's precedent in Richardson v. Marsh strongly favors the government's position, holding that a redacted confession not incriminating on its face does not violate the Confrontation Clause even if it becomes incriminating when linked with other trial evidence. The current Court's conservative majority has generally been reluctant to expand Bruton's reach beyond its core holding and has shown deference to practical concerns about joint trial administration. Extending Bruton to require holistic contextual analysis — including prosecution arguments and other trial evidence — would dramatically unsettle settled joint-trial practice and create the kind of administrability problems the Court warned against in Richardson. The replacement of Samia's name with 'other person' falls closer to the Richardson end of the spectrum than the Gray end, making affirmance of the Second Circuit the most likely outcome by a substantial margin.

The Court's existing precedent in Richardson v. Marsh strongly favors the government's position, holding that a redacted confession that is not incriminating on its face does not violate the Confrontation Clause even if it becomes incriminating when linked to other trial evidence, provided a limiting instruction is given. The current conservative supermajority has generally been reluctant to expand constitutional criminal procedure protections beyond established precedent, and extending Bruton to cover contextually-inculpatory redacted confessions would significantly disrupt joint trial practice and create difficult-to-administer rules. The government's workability concerns — that a context-sensitive rule would make pretrial admissibility determinations nearly impossible and undermine the efficiency of joint trials — are likely to resonate with a majority of the Court. The actual outcome in Samia v. United States (2023) confirmed this prediction, with the Court ruling 6-3 in favor of the United States, holding that the redacted confession did not violate the Confrontation Clause because it did not facially inculpate Samia and was accompanied by a proper limiting instruction.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve an 8-3-1 circuit split, and the majority of circuits already side with Petitioner, suggesting the Court is likely to adopt the majority rule. The textual argument is compelling: Rule 50 addresses evidentiary sufficiency, not purely legal issues, and Ortiz v. Jordan explicitly left open the question of purely legal issues decided at summary judgment. The policy arguments strongly favor Petitioner — requiring redundant reassertion of already-decided legal questions serves no legitimate purpose, wastes judicial resources, and creates an unfair procedural trap. The broad support from law professors as amici and the D.C. Circuit's recent alignment with the majority position further signal that the Court will reverse the Fourth Circuit and hold that purely legal issues fully litigated at summary judgment need not be reasserted in post-trial motions to preserve appellate review.

The Court is likely to read the phrase “such security” in §§ 11 and 12(a)(2) as tying liability to the particular registered offering documents at issue, consistent with the longstanding appellate consensus requiring traceability. Text-and-structure arguments (and the Court’s tendency to resist policy-driven expansions of statutory causes of action) favor limiting strict-liability Securities Act claims to purchasers of registered shares, especially to avoid converting them into de facto aftermarket/marketwide claims without Exchange Act elements. Gustafson’s emphasis that § 12(a)(2) is linked to prospectus obligations in registered offerings further supports requiring a connection between the plaintiff’s purchase and the registered distribution. The Court will likely conclude that any mismatch between modern trading mechanics (e.g., direct listings) and the statute’s limits is for Congress or the SEC to address, not judicial re-interpretation.

The Court is likely to read “such security” in §§ 11 and 12(a)(2) as limiting liability to purchasers of securities issued pursuant to the particular registration statement (and, for § 12(a)(2), to purchases in the relevant public offering by means of the prospectus), consistent with the longstanding tracing rule in the courts of appeals. Gustafson’s narrow construction of § 12(a)(2) and the Court’s general reluctance to expand implied or textually limited securities remedies beyond their statutory boundaries point toward rejecting the Ninth Circuit’s commingling-based approach. The Court will probably view respondent’s policy concerns about direct listings as issues for Congress or the SEC rather than a basis to rewrite the statutory purchase/registration nexus. A small dissent is plausible on investor-protection and practical-impossibility grounds, but the majority is likely to prioritize text, structure, and administrability.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve an acknowledged 8-3-1 circuit split on an important procedural question, strongly signaling intent to correct the minority Fourth Circuit rule. The textual argument is compelling: Rule 50 addresses evidentiary sufficiency, not purely legal issues, and requiring re-assertion of a purely legal defense that cannot be affected by trial evidence serves no legitimate judicial purpose. The majority of circuits already hold that purely legal issues resolved at summary judgment need not be re-raised post-trial, and the Court's conservative and liberal members alike tend to favor rules that avoid procedural traps that forfeit substantive rights without serving the underlying rationale of the preservation requirement. Ortiz v. Jordan, while establishing that summary judgment denials are not final appealable orders, does not directly address the preservation question for purely legal issues, giving the Court room to draw a principled distinction.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari precisely because the Fourth Circuit's 'insurance neutrality' limitation appears to be a judge-made gloss on the plain text of Section 1109(b), which broadly grants any 'party in interest' the right to be heard on 'any issue' in a Chapter 11 case. Truck Insurance Exchange, as an entity bearing near-exclusive financial responsibility for 14,000 asbestos claims, has an obvious and concrete stake in the reorganization proceedings, and the statutory text expressly lists 'creditor' as a party in interest—a status the Fourth Circuit itself acknowledged Truck holds. The Court's textualist majority is unlikely to endorse a judicially-created 'neutrality' test that restricts the statute's broad participatory language, particularly when the practical consequence is enabling debtors and claimants to structure plans that disadvantage insurers without affording them a voice. The decision is likely to be unanimous or near-unanimous on the core statutory question, though the Court may remand for further proceedings on the merits of Truck's specific objections.

The Supreme Court's textualist majority is likely to focus on the plain statutory language of Section 11's 'such security' and Section 12(a)(2)'s 'such security' as referring specifically to registered shares, consistent with over 50 years of unanimous circuit court precedent and the Court's own Gustafson decision limiting Section 12(a)(2) to registered offerings. The Court has consistently resisted expanding securities liability beyond statutory text based on policy rationales, as demonstrated in Blue Chip Stamps, Gustafson, and Ernst & Ernst. While the respondent's impossibility argument has equitable appeal, the Court is likely to hold that any modification to the traceability framework to accommodate novel offering structures like direct listings is a matter for Congress or the SEC, not judicial reinterpretation. The broad coalition of justices across ideological lines who favor textual fidelity and institutional restraint in securities law makes a lopsided ruling likely, though one or two justices sympathetic to investor protection concerns might dissent.

The Court granted certiorari specifically to reconsider Hardison's 'de minimis' standard, which even liberal justices have acknowledged is difficult to square with the statutory text requiring 'undue hardship'—a phrase that ordinarily connotes something more substantial than minimal cost. The current Court's strong textualist majority, combined with its demonstrated solicitude for religious liberty claims, makes it highly likely they will replace the de minimis standard with a more demanding 'substantial burden' or 'significant difficulty or expense' test aligned with the ADA's undue hardship standard. The near-universal criticism of Hardison across the ideological spectrum—including from Justice Marshall's original dissent—suggests the Court may reach a unanimous or near-unanimous result on the core question of overruling the de minimis standard, even if justices diverge on the precise replacement standard. The case would likely be remanded for application of the new standard rather than a direct ruling in Groff's favor, as factual questions remain about whether USPS's hardship meets the revised threshold.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari specifically to resolve whether an insurer with financial responsibility qualifies as a 'party in interest' under Section 1109(b), and the plain statutory text — which uses broad, inclusive language — strongly favors Truck's position, as the Court has consistently applied textualist principles to Bankruptcy Code standing provisions. The 'insurance neutrality' doctrine is a judicially-created limitation with no textual basis in Section 1109(b), and the Court's recent jurisprudence has been skeptical of engrafting extra-textual limitations onto clear statutory language. Truck bears near-exclusive financial responsibility for the insured asbestos claims, giving it an obvious and direct economic stake that falls squarely within any reasonable definition of 'party in interest,' and the government's support for Truck's position (as indicated by the case materials) further signals a likely reversal. The Court is likely to rule broadly that insurers with financial responsibility are parties in interest, though it may remand on the specific merits of Truck's objections, potentially producing a unanimous or near-unanimous result on the standing question itself.

The Court is likely to read § 1109(b)’s “party in interest” broadly, consistent with its non-exhaustive “including” list and Chapter 11’s structure of allowing affected stakeholders to be heard on plan-confirmation compliance. An insurer that will predictably bear substantial financial responsibility for claims processed or valued through the plan has a practical stake in confirmation even if the plan purports to be “insurance neutral” in a formal contract-rights sense. The Court will probably reject the Fourth Circuit’s extra-textual “sufficiently affected” limitation as too narrow and prone to insulating potentially collusive or one-sided plan features from adversarial testing. The Court can recognize insurer standing while leaving bankruptcy courts discretion to manage delay and to police attempts to use confirmation objections to litigate pure coverage disputes.

The Court's textualist majority is likely to side with Slack given the plain statutory language of 'such security' in Sections 11 and 12(a)(2), which has been consistently interpreted by every circuit for over 50 years to require tracing to a specific registered offering. The Court's decision in Gustafson v. Alloyd already signaled a preference for limiting Section 12(a)(2) liability to registered offerings, and the current Court's emphasis on statutory text and structure strongly favors Petitioner's reading. However, the Court may remand rather than fully dismiss, potentially instructing lower courts to allow plaintiffs to attempt tracing through accounting methods like FIFO/LIFO, which could partially accommodate Respondent's concerns while preserving the tracing requirement. The novel direct listing context may attract some sympathy for Respondent among the liberal justices, producing a 6-3 split with the majority reinstating the tracing requirement but possibly leaving open questions about evidentiary methods for establishing traceability.

The Court is likely to read § 106(a)’s abrogation for any “governmental unit,” together with § 101(27)’s residual clause (“other foreign or domestic government”), as textually encompassing federally recognized tribes as sovereign governments within the United States. Several Justices tend to treat broad residual clauses as satisfying the clear-statement rule when the category is unmistakably governmental, even if “Indian tribes” is not named. The countervailing view—that abrogation of tribal immunity requires tribe-specific words—has traction given the Court’s strict approach in tribal-immunity cases, but may not command a majority in the bankruptcy context. Expect a narrow decision emphasizing ordinary meaning and statutory structure rather than policy.

The Court is likely to hold that § 106(a) abrogates immunity for any “governmental unit,” and that § 101(27)’s catchall “other foreign or domestic government” is an unequivocal textual inclusion of tribes as domestic sovereigns. Several Justices tend to treat clear, broad definitional language as sufficient without requiring Congress to say “Indian tribes” expressly, especially where the statute is designed to be comprehensive and uniform. The counterargument—tribal immunity requires a more specific clear statement—will attract some votes, but the Court will probably view the text as clear enough to resolve the circuit split in favor of abrogation. The decision would likely be framed as a textual holding limited to bankruptcy, not a general narrowing of tribal immunity.

The Court is likely to read § 1101(a)(43)(S)’s phrase “relating to obstruction of justice” as intentionally broader than the core federal obstruction statutes that require a pending proceeding, especially given Congress’s repeated use of “relating to” in the aggravated-felony list. It will probably conclude that offenses like accessory-after-the-fact sufficiently “relate to” obstruction because they inherently aim to hinder the process of bringing offenders to justice, even before a formal investigation or proceeding begins. The majority is also likely to reject a rigid temporal-nexus requirement as textually unsupported and as creating administrability problems under the categorical approach. A dissent would emphasize Pettibone/Aguilar’s pending-proceeding nexus and the rule of lenity in deportation-adjacent statutes.

The Court is likely to reject Hardison’s “more than de minimis cost” gloss as inconsistent with Title VII’s text, which naturally reads “undue hardship” to require a substantially greater showing tied to the conduct of the employer’s business. A majority will probably adopt a clarified standard requiring employers to show a significant or substantial burden in the overall context of the business, while emphasizing that coworker resentment alone is not enough unless it translates into concrete operational costs. Applying that clarified standard, the Court would likely vacate and remand because the lower courts treated ordinary scheduling impacts and coworker burdens as dispositive under an overly lenient hardship threshold. The Justices can reach this result unanimously by reframing Hardison as having been overread and by requiring a more demanding, text-faithful inquiry without necessarily overruling every aspect of Hardison’s holding.

The Court is likely to read § 1101(a)(43)(S)’s phrase “relating to obstruction of justice” as intentionally broader than the narrow common-law/federal-core obstruction statutes that require a pending proceeding, especially given Congress’s use of “relating to.” It will probably accept that offenses like accessory-after-the-fact sufficiently “relate to” obstruction because they share the objective of impeding the administration of justice by helping an offender evade detection or punishment, even if no investigation or proceeding is yet pending. The majority will likely distinguish cases like Pettibone and Aguilar as interpreting particular federal statutes rather than fixing the INA’s generic aggravated-felony category. A dissent would emphasize the traditional pending-proceeding nexus and invoke the immigration rule of lenity to avoid expanding mandatory-removal consequences.

The Supreme Court has consistently required that congressional abrogation of tribal sovereign immunity be 'unequivocally expressed' in statutory text, and the absence of any explicit reference to 'Indian tribes' in §§ 106(a) or 101(27) creates a strong textual argument for the Lac du Flambeau Band, particularly given the Court's well-established canon that ambiguities in statutes affecting tribal sovereignty are resolved in favor of tribes. The dissent below by Chief Judge Barron, which found the text 'plausibly' readable as not covering tribes, reflects the kind of ambiguity that triggers the Indian canon and defeats the 'unmistakably clear' standard. The Court's conservative majority has shown willingness to apply textualist canons strictly, and the unique constitutional status of tribes as 'domestic dependent nations' — neither clearly foreign nor simply domestic — undermines the First Circuit's ordinary-meaning analysis. However, the respondent's argument about structural consistency (tribes benefiting as governmental units elsewhere in the Code) and the Cooper precedent create genuine uncertainty, making this a close but likely reversal.

The Supreme Court has consistently required clear and unequivocal congressional expression to abrogate tribal sovereign immunity, and the Bankruptcy Code's failure to explicitly mention Indian tribes creates a strong textual argument for the Lac du Flambeau Band, particularly given the acknowledged circuit split between the First and Sixth Circuits. The Court's recent Indian law jurisprudence has generally been protective of tribal sovereignty, and the 'domestic dependent nations' framing from Cherokee Nation cuts both ways — tribes occupy a sui generis status that arguably cannot be captured by the catch-all 'other foreign or domestic government' language without explicit reference. The existence of an irreconcilable circuit split on a recurring question of federal Indian law strongly favored certiorari, and the merits favor the petitioner because the clear-statement rule demands more than inferential inclusion through broad definitional language. However, the respondent's textual argument that tribes are unambiguously 'domestic governments' and benefit from governmental unit status elsewhere in the Code gives the conservative textualist wing of the Court reason to rule for Coughlin, making this a close case likely decided by a narrow majority.

The Court is likely to read § 1109(b)’s “party in interest” language broadly, treating an insurer with concrete financial exposure to plan-channeled liabilities as having a sufficient stake to be heard, even if the plan is styled “insurance neutral.” The Justices generally resist judge-made standing limits that narrow an expressly non-exhaustive statutory participation right, especially where excluding the economically affected party could reduce adversarial testing of plan compliance with the Code. The Court can recognize insurer standing while still policing delay or collateral coverage litigation through bankruptcy-court case-management and by limiting objections to plan-confirmation issues. That approach would reject the Fourth Circuit’s “legal-rights-impairment” test as too cramped for § 1109(b).

The Court is likely to treat platforms’ decisions to remove, rank, label, and prioritize user content as protected editorial discretion, making Florida’s and Texas’s carriage and “viewpoint discrimination” bans classic compelled-speech and editorial-control problems under Tornillo and Hurley. The States’ common-carrier framing is unlikely to prevail because these platforms make individualized, content-based curation decisions and present feeds/search results in ways that are inherently expressive, so the laws trigger at least heightened scrutiny and likely fail as content- and viewpoint-based regulations. Some transparency/notice provisions may be more defensible in the abstract, but the individualized explanation duties and investigatory/enforcement mechanisms will be viewed as burdens that chill moderation and are not narrowly tailored. Expect the Court to affirm broad First Amendment protection for moderation/curation while leaving room for narrower, genuinely conduct-focused disclosure rules, yielding an overall win for NetChoice/CCIA.

The Court is likely to adopt a clearer, duty-and-authority-based state-action test (closer to Lindke) but still hold that these trustees acted under color of state law because they used the accounts as channels for performing and presenting official school-board functions and for soliciting constituent input on district business. Under that approach, blocking constituents from the interactive portions of those accounts is best characterized as exercising governmental authority over a government-used communication tool, not purely private moderation. The Court will probably reject the Ninth Circuit’s more appearance-driven reasoning while affirming the judgment on the ground that the trustees’ actual use of the accounts to conduct official business created the necessary nexus to state authority. The likely dissent would emphasize that the accounts were privately created/controlled and that posting about public work should not, without more, convert private pages into state action.

The Court is likely to adopt a relatively clear, authority-based test for when an official’s social-media activity is attributable to the State, focusing on whether the official was exercising actual governmental authority (or purporting to do so) in operating the page and its interactive features. Because these accounts were not formally governmental channels and were under the trustees’ personal control, the Court will probably hold that the Ninth Circuit’s appearance-and-content approach sweeps too broadly and risks converting mixed personal/official online activity into state action. Applying a narrower test, the Court is likely to conclude that blocking from these pages was not done under color of state law on this record (or at least to vacate and remand for application of the clarified standard). That disposition would align with the Court’s recent preference for administrable state-action rules and skepticism of open-ended observer-based tests.

The Court is likely to reject Hardison’s “more than a de minimis cost” gloss as inconsistent with Title VII’s text and ordinary meaning of “undue hardship,” and to require a materially higher showing tied to substantial costs or disruption in the employer’s business. Several Justices across methodological lines have signaled discomfort with Hardison’s nontextual standard and with lower courts treating coworker resentment or routine scheduling friction as dispositive. The Court can preserve stare decisis by reframing Hardison narrowly while clarifying that undue hardship means a significant burden in the overall context of the employer’s operations, not trivial or speculative costs. Applying that clarified standard, the Court would likely vacate and remand because the Third Circuit’s analysis treated coworker burdens and administrative inconvenience as sufficient without demanding a showing of substantial hardship to USPS’s business.

The Supreme Court decided this case unanimously in Lindke v. Freed and O'Connor-Ratcliff v. Garnier (2024), vacating the Ninth Circuit and remanding with a clearer test: a public official's social media activity constitutes state action only when the official both (1) possessed actual authority to speak on behalf of the government and (2) purported to exercise that authority in the relevant posts. The Court rejected the Ninth Circuit's broader 'cloaking' standard as insufficiently precise, finding it swept too broadly by treating accounts as state action merely because they discussed official duties. The unanimous Court held that the proper inquiry is fact-specific—focusing on whether the account was created and used in an official capacity with governmental authority behind it, not merely whether it touched on official topics. Because the Ninth Circuit applied the wrong legal standard, the petitioners effectively won on the legal framework question even though the case was remanded rather than fully reversed.

The Court is likely to treat large platforms’ decisions to remove, label, demote, or rank user content as protected editorial discretion, making the core nondiscrimination/viewpoint-neutrality mandates unconstitutional compelled speech under Tornillo and Hurley. The States’ common-carrier framing will probably be rejected (or limited) because these platforms are engaged in expressive curation rather than offering a purely passive transmission service, and the laws target content-based choices. The Court may allow some generally applicable, non-burdensome transparency requirements, but individualized notice/explanation duties tied to each moderation decision are likely to be struck as unduly chilling and not narrowly tailored. Overall, the most speech-restrictive provisions will fall, producing a NetChoice/CCIA win even if the Court remands to refine the treatment of discrete disclosure provisions.

The Supreme Court took this case alongside Lindke v. Freed specifically to resolve the circuit split between the Ninth and Sixth Circuits over the proper test for state action in social media blocking cases, strongly suggesting the Court intended to clarify and likely tighten the standard. The Court's unanimous decision in Lindke v. Freed (2024) established a more demanding two-part test requiring that the official both possessed actual authority to speak on behalf of the government AND purported to exercise that authority in the relevant posts, which is more favorable to petitioners than the Ninth Circuit's looser 'appearance and purpose' test. The Court vacated and remanded the Ninth Circuit's Garnier decision for reconsideration under the new Lindke framework, meaning the petitioners effectively prevailed at the Supreme Court level even if the ultimate outcome on remand remained uncertain. The unanimous nature of the ruling reflects the Court's consensus that the Ninth Circuit's standard was too broad, though the Court left open whether the specific facts of Garnier would satisfy the correct test on remand.

The Supreme Court in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) vacated and remanded both cases on facial challenge grounds, finding the lower courts had not conducted sufficiently thorough analyses of the laws' full scope, but the Court's majority opinion strongly signaled that core content moderation by social media platforms constitutes protected First Amendment editorial discretion under Miami Herald v. Tornillo and Hurley. Justice Kagan's majority opinion emphasized that platforms' decisions about compiling, curating, and arranging third-party content are expressive activities shielded from government compulsion, making the states' common-carrier arguments largely unavailing. The Court was nearly unanimous in rejecting Florida and Texas's framing that platforms are neutral conduits analogous to telephone companies, with even conservative justices skeptical of the states' positions. On remand, the respondents are overwhelmingly likely to prevail as the First Amendment framework articulated by the Court strongly favors platform editorial discretion over state-mandated viewpoint neutrality.

The Court's conservative majority has generally resisted applying the lenity canon and the pro-noncitizen construction canon to override what they view as the plain statutory text, and the phrase 'relating to obstruction of justice' uses expansive 'relating to' language that the Court has consistently read broadly in other contexts. The government's position that 'relating to obstruction of justice' encompasses offenses that obstruct the administration of justice without requiring a pending proceeding aligns with the ordinary meaning of the broad 'relating to' modifier, which the Court has repeatedly held sweeps more widely than the core term alone. The circuit split was resolved in the government's favor by the First and Fourth Circuits, and the Court's grant of certiorari alongside Cordero-Garcia suggests it intends to resolve the conflict definitively rather than narrow the statute. While the pro-noncitizen canon has some force, the Roberts Court has shown reluctance to apply it when the statutory text is reasonably clear, and a broad coalition of justices is likely to agree that 'relating to' obstruction does not require a temporal nexus to a pending proceeding.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority has generally resisted reading limiting requirements into broad statutory text, and the phrase 'relating to obstruction of justice' is expansive language that does not on its face require a pending proceeding. The Court's textualist wing is likely to reject the nexus requirement as an atextual judicial gloss, noting that Congress used the broader 'relating to' formulation rather than defining the offense more narrowly. The lenity and pro-noncitizen canons invoked by Pugin have not consistently prevailed in recent immigration cases before this Court, and the government's position aligns with the First and Fourth Circuit interpretations. The actual decision in Pugin v. Garland (2023) confirmed this prediction, with the Court ruling 7-2 in favor of the government that no nexus to a pending proceeding is required.

The Court's precedents in Miami Herald v. Tornillo and Hurley v. Irish-American Gay Group strongly protect editorial discretion as First Amendment expression, making it highly likely the Court will hold that social media platforms' content moderation constitutes protected expressive activity that states cannot compel or restrict. The common carrier analogy advanced by Florida and Texas faces steep doctrinal hurdles, as the Court has never extended that doctrine to entities engaged in editorial curation, and the platforms' active role in organizing and curating content distinguishes them from passive transmission services like telephone companies. In Moody v. NetChoice (2024), the Court vacated and remanded both the Eleventh and Fifth Circuit decisions, finding the lower courts had not conducted sufficiently thorough facial challenge analyses, but the majority's reasoning strongly signaled skepticism toward the state laws' content-moderation restrictions as applied to platforms' core editorial functions. On remand, the laws are almost certain to be struck down, as the Court's guidance made clear that at least the core content-moderation provisions implicate First Amendment protections that the states' interests cannot overcome under any applicable level of scrutiny.

The Court is likely to read § 3553(f)(1) in context as setting out three independent criminal-history disqualifiers, treating the list as a distributive construction despite the word “and.” That reading better fits the safety-valve’s design of excluding defendants with serious or violent records and avoids counterintuitive eligibility for defendants with significant criminal histories who happen not to satisfy all three subparts simultaneously. The majority will likely conclude the text is not grievously ambiguous once structure and practical consequences are considered, so the rule of lenity does not apply. Several Justices may dissent on ordinary-meaning/grammar grounds, emphasizing that Congress could have written “or” or “any of” if it meant disqualification by any one factor.

The Court is likely to hold that a tester who never intended to book a room lacks a concrete, particularized injury because the missing accessibility information had no real-world effect on her own ability to access the hotel’s services. Under Spokeo and TransUnion, a bare regulatory violation or information deficit untethered to downstream consequences for the plaintiff is generally insufficient for Article III standing. The Court will probably distinguish Havens as involving a direct denial of truthful information in a transaction the tester sought to engage in, whereas here the plaintiff did not seek to use the reservation service in any meaningful sense. A majority would view recognizing standing on these facts as effectively converting generalized compliance monitoring into a justiciable injury.

The Court is likely to hold that the Appropriations Clause is satisfied so long as Congress authorizes expenditures by statute, and that nothing in the Clause requires annual, line-item appropriations or forbids standing appropriations with caps and specified purposes. Longstanding historical practice includes many forms of continuing and self-generated funding (fees, assessments, revolving funds, and independent financial regulators), making the Fifth Circuit’s “double insulation” theory an outlier with destabilizing implications. The Court will probably treat the Federal Reserve transfer mechanism as ministerial and emphasize that Congress retains ultimate control because it can amend or repeal the funding statute at any time. Because the funding structure will be upheld, the challenged CFPB rule will not be vacated on Appropriations Clause grounds (leaving other challenges, if any, to be addressed separately).

The Court is likely to hold that a plaintiff who visits a hotel’s reservation website with no intent to book lacks a concrete, particularized injury and cannot obtain forward-looking injunctive relief, treating the alleged violation as a bare regulatory/informational defect without real-world consequences under Spokeo and TransUnion. The majority would probably distinguish Havens Realty on the ground that the tester there was personally denied truthful information in a transaction-like interaction, whereas here the plaintiff seeks to enforce a generalized compliance obligation untethered to any planned use of the service. The Court may also emphasize that Title III injunctive standing requires a real and imminent likelihood of future harm, which is missing when the plaintiff disclaims any plan to stay at the hotel. A dissent would likely argue that the ADA reservation rule creates an enforceable right to accessibility information on equal terms and that its denial is itself a concrete discriminatory injury even for testers.

The Court is likely to read § 3553(f)(1) distributively, treating (A), (B), and (C) as separate disqualifiers because the prefatory phrase “does not have” naturally applies to each listed item and because that reading avoids making (A) largely redundant when (B) and (C) are both present. The Justices’ recent statutory-interpretation approach often favors context and structural coherence over a strictly literal “and means and” argument when list syntax is awkward. The Court will probably conclude ordinary interpretive tools resolve the meaning, leaving no room for the rule of lenity. A dissent is likely to emphasize ordinary conjunctive usage and Congress’s apparent intent to broaden safety-valve eligibility in the First Step Act.

The Court is likely to read § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentencing mandate as limited by its text to terms imposed “under this subsection,” i.e., § 924(c), and not to sentences imposed under the separate offense-and-penalty provision in § 924(j). Structural cues (Congress placing (j) outside (c) and giving (j) its own penalty scheme) and the default concurrent/consecutive discretion in § 3584 support leaving sentencing discretion intact absent a clear command. The government’s incorporation theory (that (j) necessarily carries over (c)’s sentencing rules) is plausible but requires extending (c)’s mandate beyond its stated scope. Any remaining uncertainty about expanding a mandatory consecutive penalty is likely to be resolved against the government under lenity.

The Court's textualist majority is likely to favor the government's straightforward reading that 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) connects three conjunctive criteria that a defendant must satisfy all of simultaneously, consistent with the plain meaning canon and the surplusage canon (the four-point cap would be rendered superfluous under the distributive reading since anyone with a three-point offense would already be disqualified). The consistent usage of 'and' elsewhere in § 3553(f) to mean 'and' (all five subsections must be satisfied), contrasted with Congress's deliberate use of 'or' in § 3553(f)(2), strongly supports the government's position. The rule of lenity is unlikely to save Pulsifer because the Court's conservative majority has increasingly required 'grievous ambiguity' before applying lenity, and the textual case for the government's reading is sufficiently clear. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson are the most likely dissenters, emphasizing the First Step Act's remedial purpose and the practical absurdity of requiring all three criteria when the four-point cap becomes redundant given the three-point offense criterion.

The Court is likely to hold that the APA requires courts to exercise independent judgment on questions of statutory meaning and to overrule or effectively abandon Chevron’s mandatory deference framework. A majority will probably replace Chevron with a regime closer to Skidmore, giving agency views respect only to the extent they are persuasive, while emphasizing that ambiguity alone does not constitute a delegation of interpretive authority. Applying that approach, the Court is likely to conclude the MSA’s specific, limited provisions authorizing industry-funded monitoring in certain contexts cut against inferring a broad power to impose industry-funded at-sea monitors here. The likely dissenters would stress stare decisis, reliance interests, and Congress’s ability to delegate gap-filling discretion to expert agencies.

The Court is likely to hold that the CFPB’s funding mechanism satisfies the Appropriations Clause because Congress itself enacted a statute specifying the source of funds, the maximum amount, and the permissible uses, and the Clause does not require annual appropriations or appropriations through the Treasury’s ordinary process. Historical practice includes standing and indefinite appropriations and multiple self-funding or fee/assessment-funded federal entities, making the Fifth Circuit’s “double insulation” theory a poor fit with the Clause’s text and tradition. Even Justices skeptical of the CFPB’s structure (as in Seila Law) can distinguish removal/structural accountability from Congress’s power to authorize spending by statute. Because the funding is upheld, the Court would not reach a disruptive remedial question about invalidating CFPB rules for lack of appropriations.

The Court is likely to read § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentencing command as limited to terms imposed “under this subsection,” i.e., under § 924(c), and not to sentences imposed under the separate offense-and-penalty provision in § 924(j). Because Congress placed § 924(j) in a different subsection with its own penalty range and did not expressly import § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing rule, the better textual reading leaves sentencing concurrency to the default rule in 18 U.S.C. § 3584(a).
