The conservative majority is likely to hold that flipping the default rule, so that carry is presumptively banned on most property open to the public, effectively nullifies the public-carry right Bruen recognized, while leaving owners free to exclude guns themselves. The three liberal justices would likely dissent, stressing property owners' right to exclude and the state's latitude to set background defaults.

The Sentencing Reform Act sets out a detailed scheme. Section 3624(e) gives one express tolling rule, for imprisonment of 30 or more days, and § 3583(i) gives a specific warrant-or-summons mechanism for adjudicating violations after the term expires. That structure strongly suggests Congress did not leave room for a judge-made, open-ended 'extension' doctrine that can even push the term past the statutory maximum. Even courts adopting fugitive tolling concede it has no textual basis, and this textualist Court is likely to say the government's policy concerns are adequately met by § 3583(i) warrants, new prosecution, and revocation for the absconding itself. Some justices may still find the common-law escape principle of Anderson v. Corall and the purposive reasoning of Johnson and Mont persuasive, which could produce a dissent.

The Sentencing Reform Act spells out when a supervised-release term stops running: § 3624(e) tolls it only for imprisonment of 30 or more days. Separately, § 3583(i) preserves the court's power to revoke after expiration if a warrant or summons issued during the term. That structure strongly suggests Congress did not leave room for a judge-made, open-ended fugitive-tolling rule that could stretch the term past the statutory maximum. A textualist majority is likely to stress that the government already has adequate remedies: revocation for the absconding itself, separate prosecution of new crimes, and consideration of post-expiration conduct under § 3553(a). The government's common-law and 'no profit from wrongdoing' arguments may draw a dissent, but they probably cannot overcome the statute's detailed scheme.

The Court will likely treat the plea agreement as a contract under Puckett and Santobello and hold that Hunter's broad waiver, which excepted only ineffective-assistance claims, plainly covers a due-process challenge to a foreseeable supervised-release condition. The Court may say, consistent with Garza, that some exceptions exist without endorsing the Fifth Circuit's rigid two-exception rule, but it will find this claim falls within the waiver. On the second question, a routine end-of-sentencing statement by the judge cannot unilaterally modify a written agreement, and the government's silence is not mutual assent or a knowing relinquishment of its rights. Some justices, especially the liberal bloc and possibly Gorsuch, may favor broader exceptions or a remand, so a narrow or fractured opinion is possible.

The Court limited review to the private-property default rule, and the federal government supported petitioners; both signal that the Court is inclined to reverse a Ninth Circuit ruling that conflicts with the Second Circuit's decision in Antonyuk. Hawaii's rule flips the traditional presumption, so licensed carry becomes unlawful across most public-facing places unless the owner consents. That looks like an end-run around Bruen's holding that the right to carry extends to public spaces generally. The State's main analogues are thin: a 1771 New Jersey anti-poaching law aimed at enclosed lands and an 1865 Louisiana Black Code provision with discriminatory origins. These are likely to be found neither 'well-established and representative' nor relevantly similar in 'how and why' they burdened the right. The conservative majority will likely hold the default rule unconstitutional, perhaps adding guidance on the analogue inquiry, while the three liberal justices dissent and stress property owners' rights and the 'historical twin' caution from Rahimi.

The Court's arm-of-the-State precedents, especially Hess and Regents, treat the State's legal liability for judgments as the most salient factor, and New Jersey has expressly made NJ Transit a separate corporation that is liable for its own debts and can sue and be sued. Historical practice supports the injured plaintiffs, since separately incorporated public enterprises such as founding-era banks and municipalities were not treated as sharing the State's immunity. Several Justices are also likely to resist letting a State unilaterally extend constitutional immunity through its own labels and executive-control structures, particularly for ordinary torts committed on other States' roads. NJ Transit's arguments about state control, dignity, and practical fiscal impact may attract a couple of votes, but most Justices are likely to hold NJ Transit is not an arm of the State, reversing Pennsylvania and affirming New York.

I predict the Court will hold that NJ Transit is not an arm of New Jersey for interstate immunity purposes, so Galette prevails. Hess and Regents v. Doe make the State's legal liability for judgments the most salient factor, and New Jersey chose to make NJ Transit a separate 'sue and be sued' corporation whose judgments do not bind the treasury. New Jersey also excluded NJ Transit from the definition of 'State' in its Tort Claims Act, so honoring that structure hardly offends New Jersey's dignity, especially where the suits involve torts committed within the forum States. Some justices may favor a more holistic, dignity-focused test that weighs the State's characterization and control, which could produce dissents.

The Court granted review despite repeatedly denying certiorari on appeal-waiver questions, and even the government does not fully defend the Fifth Circuit's rigid two-exception rule, arguing mainly that the outcome is correct 'under any standard.' That makes it likely the Court will reject the closed two-exception framework, holding that contract principles and public-policy limits (as in Garza and Rumery) permit other exceptions. It would then probably vacate and remand for the Fifth Circuit to apply the correct standard. The second question, the Ninth Circuit's judge-advisement rule, is weaker and likely to be rejected or left unaddressed, so the petitioner's win may be narrow.

Tanzin's textual reasoning strongly favors Landor, and the facts are egregious; the United States also supports him. But RLUIPA rests on the Spending Clause rather than Congress's plenary power over federal officers. Several conservative justices have shown interest in the contract analogy and the Pennhurst clear-notice rule (see Cummings and Talevski), which supports the argument that non-party officials cannot be personally bound by funding conditions. With unanimous circuit agreement and Sossamon reading 'appropriate relief' as ambiguous in the Spending Clause context, a narrow conservative majority will likely affirm, with the liberal justices dissenting.

Read naturally, § 1391's 'as of the end of the plan year' fixes the date as of which unfunded vested benefits are measured; it does not set a deadline for the actuary to adopt assumptions, and valuations are routinely completed after the measurement date. Section 1393(a)'s 'best estimate' and 'reasonable in the aggregate' requirements, together with arbitral review, are the safeguards Congress chose against manipulation, which undercuts the need for an atextual freeze rule like Metz's. The United States/PBGC's support for the Fund and the practical risks of locking in stale assumptions should appeal to the Court's textualists and its pragmatists alike. Some Justices may still be persuaded by the employers' concerns about predictability and hindsight-driven manipulation, which could produce a dissent.

The ordinary meaning of computing liability 'as of' a date contemplates a retrospective calculation using inputs that may be finalized later, so the text supports the Fund. The statute imposes no deadline for adopting actuarial assumptions, and actuarial practice routinely completes valuations after the valuation date. The Solicitor General and PBGC back this reading, and the Court is likely to view the manipulation concerns as adequately addressed by the 'best estimate' requirement of § 1393 and arbitral review under § 1401. Expect a unanimous affirmance holding that assumptions may be selected after the measurement date if based on information available as of that date.

Tanzin gives petitioner a strong textual argument, but RLUIPA's prison provisions rest on the Spending Clause. Under the Court's Pennhurst, Barnes, and Cummings line, that framework treats funding conditions as contract-like, binding only the recipients who accept them and requiring unambiguous notice. Sossamon already held that 'appropriate relief' is too ambiguous to clearly authorize damages against the State, and every circuit to address the question has rejected individual-capacity damages. A majority of the conservative justices therefore seems likely to hold that non-recipient state officers cannot be held personally liable under a Spending Clause statute, while condemning the conduct and inviting Congress to act, with the three liberal justices (and possibly Gorsuch) dissenting.

Coy and Craig squarely require a case-specific finding that a screen is necessary to protect the particular child from trauma caused by the defendant's presence, and a mandatory statute is exactly the kind of 'legislatively imposed presumption of trauma' that Coy forbids. The trial court relied on the statute's 'shall' language rather than any evidentiary finding, and Mississippi is an outlier among jurisdictions on this question. That makes the case a strong candidate for a per curiam summary reversal enforcing vertical precedent. On harmlessness, the Court likely either rejects the Mississippi Supreme Court's analysis or remands for a proper Chapman inquiry, since that analysis leaned on evidence Pitts arguably introduced only because of the error.

With the Solicitor General backing Monsanto, a circuit split to resolve, and a Court generally receptive to text-based uniformity arguments, a majority is likely to read § 136v(b) as barring states from imposing, through jury verdicts, a cancer warning that EPA has determined through registration and label approval is unwarranted and that Monsanto could not add on its own. The majority can do this while preserving Bates's parallel-requirements framework, by holding that a duty that diverges from EPA's authoritative labeling determinations is not 'genuinely equivalent' to FIFRA's misbranding standard. Justices Gorsuch and Thomas are skeptical of implied and purposes-based preemption, so the express-preemption route is more likely to command a majority than the impossibility theory, though Gorsuch could defect. The liberal Justices will likely dissent, relying on Bates, Wyeth, and § 136a(f)(2)'s statement that registration is no defense to misbranding.

On reargument, the conservative majority signaled skepticism that Section 2, as applied through Gingles to require intentional creation of an additional majority-minority district, can justify race-predominant line-drawing under strict scrutiny, especially where the remedy rests only on a preliminary-injunction finding. District 6's 250-mile configuration linking distant Black populations makes the racial-predominance finding hard to disturb under clear-error review, and Louisiana itself has abandoned its defense of the map. The Court is likely to affirm the three-judge court, either by holding that Section 2 compliance did not supply a compelling interest here or by significantly narrowing Gingles and Allen v. Milligan in redistricting. The three liberal justices would dissent, defending Section 2's results test and Milligan.

Coy and Craig squarely hold that a screen blocking a child witness's view of the defendant requires a case-specific finding that this child would be traumatized by the defendant's presence; a mandatory statute's legislative presumption of trauma cannot substitute for that finding. Here the trial judge applied the screen solely because the statute says 'shall,' and the record suggests the child wanted to see her father. The Mississippi Supreme Court therefore openly departed from binding precedent, which makes summary reversal per curiam likely. The Court would probably decline to decide harmlessness itself and remand, as it did in Coy, letting the state courts apply Chapman without the tainted testimony.

The Court granted review over an entrenched split, and the Solicitor General's support for Monsanto signals that EPA treats a cancer warning as misbranding; that makes the respondent's 'parallel requirements' theory under Bates hard to sustain. FIFRA, unlike the drug regime in Wyeth, has no changes-being-effected mechanism, so Monsanto could not add the warning unilaterally. That brings the case closer to Mensing's impossibility logic and strengthens the express-preemption argument that Missouri imposed a requirement 'in addition to or different from' federal law. Textualists such as Thomas and Gorsuch may resist reading agency registration decisions as preemptive 'requirements' (given § 136a(f)(2) and Bates), and they may join the liberal justices, but a majority led by Roberts, Alito, Kavanaugh and Barrett will likely find preemption.

The Court ordered reargument on whether intentionally creating a majority-minority district violates the Constitution, which signals that the conservative majority is skeptical of using Section 2 compliance to justify race-predominant districting. Louisiana's own abandonment of its defense of SB8 undercuts the appellants' position. District 6's 250-mile configuration and the absence of a final Section 2 merits ruling make it hard to show narrow tailoring or a strong basis in evidence. The likely result is that a majority affirms the district court's racial-gerrymander holding, either by sharply narrowing how Gingles-based Section 2 compliance can justify race-based districts or by invalidating that justification as applied, with the three liberal justices dissenting.

After Rahimi, the Court is unlikely to endorse the Fifth Circuit's rule that only people intoxicated at the moment of possession may be disarmed, because that demands something close to a historical twin. Founding-era laws on habitual drunkards and on the dangerous can support temporarily disarming a category of people whose ongoing condition makes them presently risky with firearms. Several justices, however, will likely worry about the breadth and vagueness of 'unlawful user,' especially for occasional marijuana users. The most likely outcome is therefore a narrower holding, upholding the statute as applied to regular, habitual users like Hemani and vacating or reversing the Fifth Circuit, with dissents or concurrences pressing for limits.

Rahimi's 'relevantly similar' approach and its endorsement of disarming categories of persons who present a special danger of misuse give the government a workable path. Founding-era habitual-drunkard laws imposed burdens (vagrancy confinement, commitment, sureties) arguably heavier than temporary disarmament. Even so, several Justices appear uneasy with categorically disarming sober marijuana users, so the Court will likely reject a broad ruling and narrow the statute's reach to habitual, regular users who pose an ongoing risk. Because Hemani's record (habitual use of marijuana and allegedly other drugs) likely fits that narrower category, the Court will probably vacate the Fifth Circuit's as-applied invalidation, though a ruling for respondent is a real possibility.

The Court will likely accept, or assume, that a negligent-selection claim relates to broker 'services' under Rowe and Dan's City. It should then hold the claim saved by §14501(c)(2)(A), because common-law tort duties are part of a State's 'safety regulatory authority' under Cipollone, Riegel and Ours Garage. A claim aimed at keeping unsafe trucks and drivers off highways is plausibly 'with respect to motor vehicles,' even when the defendant is a broker. Textualist and federalism-minded justices (e.g., Thomas, Gorsuch, Barrett), joined by the liberal bloc, are likely to resist a reading that leaves injured motorists with no remedy, while some justices may side with the Seventh and Eleventh Circuits' narrower, vehicle-focused reading of the exception.

Ours Garage already read the safety exception broadly, as preserving states' traditional police power over highway safety, and the Court routinely treats common-law duties as a form of state 'regulation' (Cipollone, Riegel). A negligent-selection claim aimed at keeping unsafe trucks and drivers off public roads fits naturally within the expansive phrase 'with respect to motor vehicles,' even though brokers themselves do not operate vehicles. Several textualist and federalism-minded justices (e.g., Gorsuch, Barrett, Thomas) are wary of reading express preemption clauses to wipe out traditional tort remedies, and the coalition of 29 states plus D.C. reinforces that concern. Some justices may nonetheless be persuaded by the respondents' structural argument that brokers were deliberately left out of the exception and by supply-chain concerns, producing a dissent.

The federal Election Day statutes only fix the day of the 'election,' and Foster v. Love's 'final selection' definition is plausibly satisfied when voters irrevocably cast their ballots by that day; receipt and counting are administrative steps that have always continued after Election Day. Long-standing historical practice of post-Election Day receipt, together with Congress's evident awareness and acquiescence (including UOCAVA, the MOVE Act, and the ECRA), weighs heavily against reading an implied receipt deadline into a century-old statute. That reading would also disrupt the election rules of roughly half the states, which matters given the states' primary authority over the manner of elections. Some textualist justices (likely Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch) may accept the RNC's 'consummation' reading, but Roberts, Kavanaugh, Barrett and the liberal justices are likely to reverse the Fifth Circuit.

The Election Day statutes fix only the day of the 'election,' and Foster v. Love's concern was elections consummated *before* that day. Reading the statutes to bar counting ballots cast by Election Day but received later fits awkwardly with long-standing practice in many states, with UOCAVA's express accommodation of late-arriving military ballots, and with the Elections Clause's default grant of 'manner' authority to states. A textualist majority, likely including the Chief Justice, Barrett, and possibly Kavanaugh joining the liberal justices, will probably read 'election' as the voters' final choice being made by Election Day, while Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch would adopt the Fifth Circuit's receipt-based reading. Given the federal government's and the RNC's historical-meaning arguments, the outcome is genuinely uncertain.

The Court took Cox's petition, with the Solicitor General's support, and denied the labels' cross-petition on vicarious liability, which suggests it means to narrow the Fourth Circuit's broad 'knowledge plus material contribution' standard. Sony, Grokster, and Twitter v. Taamneh all point toward requiring culpable intent, meaning inducement or a service tailored to infringement, rather than mere knowing provision of a general-purpose service such as internet access. Several justices are likely to worry that the labels' rule would force ISPs to cut off households, hospitals, and universities on the strength of automated notices, though some may read the DMCA safe harbor as assuming liability exists. The most likely result is reversal with a remand, perhaps leaving room for liability on more culpable facts; the Court may also adopt the standard civil willfulness rule (knowledge or reckless disregard of one's own illegality) or find that issue unnecessary to reach.

TAMA recognized a limited private rescission remedy under the nearly identical, simultaneously enacted IAA § 215. The 1980 amendment adding 'a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party' makes the ICA's textual case for a rescission-only action even stronger. A textualist majority can therefore affirm without retreating from Sandoval, treating the right as grounded in text rather than policy and confining it to rescission. The SEC's opposition and the Court's general hostility to implied actions keep the outcome uncertain, with several conservative justices possibly finding § 47(b) merely defensive.

Dolan already read the postal exception to cover injuries arising because mail 'fails to arrive at all,' and the text attaches 'negligent' only to 'transmission,' which leaves 'loss' and 'miscarriage' broad enough to cover mail deliberately withheld from the addressee. The Court's textualist majority is likely to hold that the claim arises out of mail not reaching its destination regardless of the carrier's motive. They will also likely note that sovereign-immunity waivers are construed in favor of the sovereign and that Congress meant to shield the Postal Service's core delivery function from tort suits. Concerns about leaving victims without a remedy, pressed by amici, will likely draw a dissent from justices such as Jackson, Sotomayor, and perhaps Gorsuch, but probably not enough votes to affirm.

The Court will most likely hold that IEEPA's power to 'regulate ... importation' does not include the power to impose tariffs. Three points support that reading: tariffs are a taxing power the Constitution assigns to Congress, IEEPA never mentions duties, and every other tariff delegation (such as the Trade Act of 1974) is explicit and limited. Major-questions and nondelegation concerns about unlimited, unreviewable tariff power reinforce this reading, and BP v. Baltimore undercuts the government's ratification argument built on the single Yoshida decision. The Court may still agree with the government that the Court of International Trade, not the district court, has exclusive jurisdiction, which would vacate the D.D.C. judgment in No. 24-1287, but on the central merits question the challengers should prevail, with Justices Thomas, Alito and Kavanaugh likely dissenting.

This is a close call. The Court is generally hostile to implied rights of action, and the SEC supports petitioners, which favors the funds. But TAMA held that near-identical voiding language in the companion Investment Advisers Act supports a limited private rescission action, and Congress then added the more explicit phrase "rescission at the instance of any party" to § 47(b) the following year. Textualist justices are therefore likely to read the provision as an express, narrow rescission remedy confined to contracting parties, which satisfies Sandoval without any judicial implication and makes the Second Circuit's affirmance the likelier outcome.

Under the Hanna/Shady Grove framework, the threshold question is whether a Federal Rule answers the question in dispute, and Rule 8 (with Rules 9, 11 and 12) defines what a complaint must contain and when a claim may be dismissed for pleading deficiencies, leaving no room for a state requirement that an expert affidavit accompany the complaint. Rule 8 is plainly a valid procedural rule under the Rules Enabling Act, so it controls regardless of Delaware's substantive motivations. Respondents' attempt to recharacterize the affidavit as a substantive element or burden of proof is undercut by the statute's timing (filed with the complaint) and its pleading-stage dismissal remedy. The growing circuit consensus (2d, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th) and the Court's textualist approach to the Federal Rules suggest a lopsided reversal of the Third Circuit, perhaps with separate writings on the methodology.

Dolan described the postal exception as retaining immunity for harms that arise because mail 'fails to arrive at all or arrives late... or at the wrong address,' which squarely describes Konan's injury regardless of the employee's motive. On ordinary meaning, 'miscarriage' (mail failing to reach its intended destination) does not obviously depend on intent, and 'negligent' most naturally modifies only 'transmission.' The government's concerns that the exception could be pleaded around and that the FTCA was meant to protect postal operations will likely appeal to the textualist and government-protective justices. Konan's 'no one intentionally loses something' argument and the remedial-gap concerns could attract Gorsuch and the liberal justices, producing a close split.

On the merits, a majority is likely to hold that IEEPA's power to 'regulate ... importation' does not include the distinct power to lay duties. Key factors are the statute's silence on tariffs, nearly 50 years without a President using it for tariffs, the expressly limited tariff delegations Congress wrote in the Trade Act of 1974, and major-questions and nondelegation concerns about reading it to allow unlimited tariffs. The Yoshida ratification argument is weak under BP v. Baltimore, so it should not carry the government, though Justices Thomas, Alito and Kavanaugh may dissent on foreign-affairs deference grounds. The main risk to petitioners is jurisdiction: the Court could find that tariff challenges belong exclusively to the CIT under § 1581(i), vacating the D.D.C. judgment in No. 24-1287 while affirming the Federal Circuit's merits ruling in V.O.S. Selections.

Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the first question is whether a valid Federal Rule answers the question in dispute. Rules 8, 9, and 12 together define what a plaintiff must file to state a claim and survive dismissal at the outset, and the Delaware statute adds a different, conflicting requirement. Most circuits (the Second, Fourth, Sixth, Seventh and Ninth) agree that such affidavit statutes collide with the Rules, and the Court's text-focused approach to the Rules suggests it will join them rather than adopt the Third Circuit's narrow 'different purpose' reading. Some Justices may concur only in the judgment on the Rules Enabling Act or substantive-versus-procedural reasoning, but a lopsided majority for Berk is likely.

The Court's recent unanimous aiding-and-abetting decisions in Twitter v. Taamneh and Smith & Wesson stress that knowingly providing a generally available service, without culpable participation, is not secondary liability, and Grokster and Sony point the same way. The Solicitor General also backs Cox, and the Court granted Cox's petition while denying the labels' cross-petition, which signals interest in narrowing the Fourth Circuit's 'knowledge plus continued service' rule. Several justices are likely uneasy with Cox's record, including its thirteen-strike policy and its contempt for the DMCA, and some may also worry that Cox's rule would make the DMCA safe harbor meaningless. Even so, a majority will likely hold that mere knowledge of subscriber infringement plus continued general internet access does not establish contributory liability, and will reverse and remand, possibly leaving room for a narrower intent-based theory.

Both the petitioner and the United States agree that MVRA restitution is criminal punishment. Its text, structure and enforcement all mark it as criminal: it sits in Title 18, is imposed as part of the sentence for a conviction, and is enforced through probation, supervised release and contempt. The Court's prior descriptions of restitution in Pasquantino, Paroline and Kelly point the same way, so the Smith v. Doe intent inquiry readily favors treating it as penal. The Court will likely hold MVRA restitution is punishment for Ex Post Facto purposes, vacate, and remand the question of whether the extended collection period actually increased punishment, with possible concurrences (e.g., Thomas) on the broader Ex Post Facto framework.

Both parties agree that MVRA restitution is criminal punishment. The statutory text and structure strongly support that view: it sits in Title 18, is imposed as part of the sentence only upon conviction, is labeled a 'penalty,' and is enforced through criminal mechanisms. Precedents such as Pasquantino and Paroline already describe this restitution as punitive, so the Court likely resolves the case at the first step of Smith v. Doe based on congressional intent, rejecting the appointed amicus's civil-remedy theory. The Court will likely vacate and remand, leaving to the lower courts whether retroactive application actually increased Ellingburg's punishment, with possible concurrences on the original meaning of the Ex Post Facto Clause.

Perry v. Leeke already stated that a testifying defendant has no constitutional right to consult counsel about his ongoing testimony, and the order here preserved consultation on every other subject, which distinguishes it from the total ban in Geders. A majority will likely read the Sixth Amendment as protecting access to counsel's assistance, not a right to midstream coaching. Several justices appeared receptive to treating a narrowly drawn order as permissible, perhaps one barring 'managing' testimony while tolerating incidental discussion tied to strategy or plea decisions. Liberal justices may dissent on workability and chilling grounds, citing Perry's own acknowledgment that overnight discussions inevitably touch on testimony.

Perry v. Leeke already says a testifying defendant has no constitutional right to discuss his ongoing testimony with counsel, while keeping a protected right to confer on other matters such as tactics, other witnesses, and plea negotiations. A topic-limited overnight order that preserves those protected discussions fits neatly within the line Geders and Perry drew, unlike Geders' total ban on communication. At argument, the justices seemed receptive to a narrow order barring counsel from 'managing' or coaching testimony, while noting that incidental discussion of testimony within strategic advice must remain permitted. The Court is therefore likely to affirm, possibly with concurrences disagreeing over the rationale or how to draw the line, rather than adopt petitioner's categorical rule.

Section 2244(b)(1) by its text reaches only habeas applications 'under section 2254,' and §2255(h) incorporates only §2244's certification procedure, not its substantive same-claim bar. That textual point, together with the government's concession and the lopsided circuit split, makes reversal on the merits likely. The harder question is jurisdiction, but a majority is likely to read §2244(b)(3)(E)'s certiorari bar as not stripping §1254(1) review of federal prisoners' §2255 authorization decisions, or as not applying to them at all. Textualist and finality-minded justices may dissent on jurisdiction, making for a close split.

Section 2244(b)(1) by its text reaches only claims in a 'habeas corpus application under section 2254,' and §2255(h)'s cross-reference to certification 'as provided in section 2244' most naturally imports the court-of-appeals authorization procedure, not the state-prisoner same-claim bar. On jurisdiction, §2244(b)(3)(E) speaks of 'applications' rather than §2255 motions and governs review of the certification decision rather than the certification itself, so a majority will likely read it narrowly and avoid stripping the Court's certiorari jurisdiction. The government's long-standing concession on the merits and the lopsided circuit split strengthen petitioner's position. Textualist and finality-minded Justices may dissent, arguing that the certiorari bar is incorporated wholesale, which would make the vote close.

A candidate has a particularized stake in the rules governing how votes in his own election are counted, which distinguishes him from the ordinary voters whose generalized grievances were rejected in Lance and Gill. The Court's recent emphasis on keeping standing simple, in Diamond Alternative Energy and FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate, supports finding a concrete injury: both the harm to electoral prospects and the monitoring costs Bost actually incurs because the counting period is extended. Applying Clapper's 'certainly impending' standard to the risk of losing the election misreads that case, since the statute's application is certain. Some justices may rest on narrower grounds, such as monitoring costs, and the more liberal justices may dissent, citing Clapper and concerns about opening the courthouse doors to election litigation.

A majority is likely to hold that candidates have a concrete, particularized interest in the rules governing how votes in their own elections are counted. That stake is distinct from the generalized grievance of voters in Lance and Gill, and it does not require showing that the rule will change the outcome. Some justices may instead rest standing on the narrower ground that Bost incurs near-certain monitoring costs, following Judge Scudder's reasoning and FEC v. Cruz rather than Clapper. Justices Jackson and Sotomayor would likely dissent, warning that this broadens standing and invites election litigation.

NIFLA rejected a low-protection 'professional speech' category, and Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project holds that a law triggered by the communicative content of words regulates speech, not conduct. As applied to purely verbal talk therapy, Colorado's law permits affirming messages but bars change-oriented ones, which the majority will likely view as content-based and arguably viewpoint-based. The Court will likely reverse the Tenth Circuit's rational-basis holding and remand for strict scrutiny, citing the contested evidence on voluntary talk therapy highlighted in Judge Hartz's dissent. Some liberal justices (e.g., Kagan) may share the viewpoint-discrimination concern, so the majority could be larger than the conservative bloc, but a 6-3 split along familiar lines is most likely.

Section 924(c)(1)(A) is plainly a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger, because § 924(j) expressly incorporates a § 924(c) violation. That triggers the presumption against cumulative punishment, which can be overcome only by a clear indication of contrary congressional intent. Section 924(c)'s 'in addition to' language reaches only the predicate crime of violence, not § 924(j), and Lora already treated § 924(j) as a distinct penalty scheme outside § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentence mandate. With the government confessing error and the Hunter analogy weak, the Court will likely hold that one conviction must be vacated, possibly with separate concurrences on the scope of the Double Jeopardy rationale.

NIFLA rejected a reduced-protection 'professional speech' category, and Humanitarian Law Project holds that when the regulated 'conduct' is itself communication, the law regulates speech. Both precedents point toward treating Chiles's pure talk therapy as speech. The statute permits counseling that affirms or supports transition but forbids counseling that aims at change, which makes it content-based and likely viewpoint-based, triggering heightened scrutiny that the Tenth Circuit never applied. The Court will likely reverse and remand for strict scrutiny, perhaps with some liberal justices (e.g., Kagan) joining on the viewpoint-discrimination rationale, while preserving states' power to regulate genuine professional conduct and malpractice.

The Court's recent habeas-channeling jurisprudence, especially Jones v. Hendrix, reflects a majority strongly committed to protecting § 2255's carefully reticulated limits (time bars, successive-motion restrictions) from circumvention through other statutory vehicles. A judge's 'disquiet' about a jury verdict he already upheld on direct review and in § 2255 proceedings is a particularly unattractive vehicle for petitioner, since it looks like a merits attack on guilt repackaged as an equitable reason, threatening jury verdicts and finality. The government's textual argument also gives the majority a clean hook: reasons that are common grounds for collateral attack are not 'extraordinary,' and Congress channeled them elsewhere. Concepcion's breadth concerns what courts may consider once a modification proceeding is properly triggered, so the Court can readily distinguish it, while the liberal justices (and possibly Gorsuch) may dissent on textual and lenity grounds.

Every § 924(j) offense requires proof of a § 924(c) violation plus a resulting death, so § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense under Blockburger. That triggers the Whalen/Rutledge/Ball presumption against cumulative convictions, and the presumption yields only to a clear statement of contrary congressional intent. Lora already held that § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)'s consecutive-sentence mandate does not reach § 924(j), which undercuts the amicus's main textual hook and leaves no clear authorization to stack both convictions. With both the defendant and the government urging vacatur, and the Court's precedents treating even an extra conviction as punishment, the Court will likely reverse, perhaps with some Justices concurring separately on Hunter or the scope of the Blockburger presumption.

The Court's recent decision in Jones v. Hendrix, along with the Preiser/Gonzalez line of cases, shows a majority committed to preventing prisoners from evading AEDPA's limits by relabeling attacks on the validity of a conviction or sentence. A district judge's doubts about a cooperator's credibility, and so about the defendant's guilt, look squarely like relitigating a jury verdict, which is the core of § 2255. The textual argument that 'extraordinary and compelling' carries only one express limit has force with some justices, possibly Gorsuch alongside the liberal wing. Even so, the majority will likely read the phrase in context, alongside the specific, exclusive § 2255 remedy, to exclude reasons that attack the validity of the conviction or sentence.

The Court's current majority has steadily narrowed the permissible campaign-finance interest to quid pro quo corruption or its appearance, as in McCutcheon, Citizens United and Cruz, which erodes Colorado II's broader anti-circumvention rationale. The government has switched sides and now agrees the limits are unconstitutional, so a Court-appointed amicus is left defending the judgment. Statutory changes since 2001 also undercut Colorado II's factual premises, including BCRA's soft-money ban and the 2014 creation of separate party accounts. The likely outcome is that the conservative majority reverses, either overruling Colorado II or distinguishing it for party-coordinated communications, with the three liberal justices dissenting on stare decisis and anti-circumvention grounds.

The Court's post-2001 campaign-finance cases, especially McCutcheon and FEC v. Cruz, narrowed the permissible government interest to quid pro quo corruption or its appearance and demanded close tailoring, which undercuts Colorado II's broad anti-circumvention rationale. Because the Solicitor General declined to defend the statute, the case was argued against a Court-appointed amicus and the DNC, so there is no executive-branch defense of the limits to draw deference. The conservative majority is likely to hold that coordinated party expenditure limits, at least as applied to party coordinated communications, violate the First Amendment, and either overrule or sharply confine Colorado II. The three liberal Justices would likely dissent, invoking stare decisis and the risk that unlimited party coordination lets donors evade contribution limits; a jurisdictional or mootness off-ramp is possible but less likely.

Brigham City and Fisher already set the test for emergency-aid entries: police need an 'objectively reasonable basis for believing' that someone inside is seriously injured or imminently threatened with injury. The Court is likely to reaffirm that standard rather than import a probable-cause requirement built for criminal investigation, though it may disavow the Montana court's looser 'community caretaker' and reasonable-suspicion phrasing. On these facts — a reported suicide threat, a sound like a gun clicking followed by silence, and signs of danger seen from outside — the entry plausibly satisfies the Brigham City standard, so the judgment would be affirmed. Justices concerned about privacy may write concurrences stressing that the standard is demanding and is not a community-caretaking loophole, but a broad or unanimous majority for Montana seems likely.

At oral argument, the justices seemed reluctant to import the criminal-investigation concept of probable cause into the emergency-aid context, where officers act to protect life rather than to find evidence of a crime. Brigham City's 'objectively reasonable basis for believing' standard is already the governing test, and the Court is likely to reaffirm it rather than relabel it, while making clear it is not a mere reasonable-suspicion or community-caretaking standard (consistent with Caniglia). On these facts — a reported suicide threat, a possible gunshot, no response at the door, and a visible empty holster — the entry was reasonable under Brigham City and Fisher. I therefore expect affirmance, likely unanimous or nearly so, with concurrences stressing the sanctity of the home and the limits of the exception.

Title III expressly defines liable 'persons' to include agencies and instrumentalities of foreign states, and § 6082(d) contemplates judgments against Cuban instrumentalities. The Act also amended the FSIA's execution-immunity rules for Title III judgments. Read together, these provisions look much like the clear, specific congressional statement that Halkbank and the Court's textualist majority treat as enough to displace a general background regime. The Solicitor General's support for Exxon and Congress's stated aim of a 'fully effective' remedy further push toward abrogation, since an FSIA-exception requirement would largely nullify suits against the very Cuban entities Congress targeted. Some justices, however, may favor FSIA exclusivity and caution about foreign-relations friction, or may adopt a narrower Cuba-specific holding, so a divided Court is likely.

Title III imposes liability on 'any person,' and § 6023(11) expressly defines 'person' to include 'any agency or instrumentality of a foreign state.' That closely parallels the definitional abrogation the Court accepted in Lac du Flambeau, and it is reinforced by Helms-Burton's simultaneous amendment of FSIA § 1611(c) to address execution of Title III judgments. The textualist majority, joined by the Executive's foreign-policy endorsement, is likely to treat this as a sufficiently clear statement, and the Cuba-specific, later-enacted statute as controlling over the FSIA's general immunity framework without any need to amend § 1605. A minority may still invoke Amerada Hess's exclusivity principle, the practice of amending the FSIA directly, and comity concerns to require an FSIA exception.

The Court has repeatedly stressed that the collateral-order doctrine is narrow and must not swallow the final-judgment rule (Will v. Hallock, Mohawk, Digital Equipment). Campbell-Ewald already signaled that contractors do not share the government's sovereign immunity. That makes Yearsley best understood as a merits defense: an agent acting within authority validly conferred by its principal is not liable, and that question can be fully reviewed after final judgment. With the Solicitor General siding with respondents and disclaiming any federal need for an immunity from suit, and with heavy factual overlap between Yearsley's 'authorized and directed' inquiry and the merits, a broad majority, likely unanimous, should affirm the Tenth Circuit.

Caterpillar rested on a genuine pre-judgment cure: the nondiverse party left through settlement, a valid and independent event. Here the only 'cure' was the district court's own erroneous, interlocutory dismissal, which merged into the final judgment and was reversed on appeal. That reversal restored the nondiverse Texas defendant, so complete diversity never existed and § 1447(c) and Finn require vacatur and remand. Most Justices are likely to be wary of letting a court manufacture its own jurisdiction through error, whatever the cost in finality and efficiency, though one or two may favor preserving the judgment against the diverse defendant.

Caterpillar rested on a cure that came from an independent event (the nondiverse defendant's settlement); it did not hold that a district court's own erroneous ruling could create the complete diversity that supports its judgment. Once the Fifth Circuit reversed the interlocutory dismissal of Whole Foods, which had merged into the final judgment, a Texas defendant was back in the case against Texas plaintiffs. Complete diversity therefore never existed at judgment, and Caterpillar itself says an uncured jurisdictional defect requires vacatur. The Court's recent strict enforcement of jurisdictional limits (Grupo Dataflux, Royal Canin) and § 1447(c)'s mandatory remand language make it likely the Court affirms, probably unanimously or nearly so, despite the efficiency concerns.

New Jersey's own brief concedes that an objectively reasonable chill from a subpoena's issuance is a ripe Article III injury that §1983 can redress in federal court. That leaves the Third Circuit's reliance on prudential ripeness and state-court adjudication vulnerable under Lexmark, Susan B. Anthony List, Knick, and the 'virtually unflagging obligation' principle. A demand for donor identities, backed by an express threat of contempt, fits squarely within the chill-is-the-harm logic of AFPF v. Bonta and NAACP v. Alabama. The Court will likely reverse and remand, holding that First Choice's First Amendment claim is ripe and need not first be litigated in state court, while leaving the merits and any abstention questions open.

Wilkinson v. Garland already signaled that reviewing courts should defer when a mixed question is primarily factual. Whether particular threats and a beating rise to 'persecution' is a case-specific weighing of severity, context, and country conditions, which is the kind of work U.S. Bank and Monasky treat as primarily factual. Section 1252(b)(4)(B) codifies the Elias-Zacarias 'compelled to conclude' standard, and the Court has applied it to persecution determinations for decades. Loper Bright addresses pure statutory interpretation, not fact-bound applications, so the Court will likely affirm the First Circuit, possibly unanimously, while preserving de novo review for genuine legal questions embedded in persecution determinations.

Section 1252(b)(4)(B) codified Elias-Zacarias's deferential standard. Whether particular mistreatment is severe enough to count as 'persecution' is a fact-intensive, case-specific mixed question, which Wilkinson indicates gets deferential review when it is primarily factual. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson address reviewability, not the standard of review, and Loper Bright concerns statutory interpretation rather than applying a statutory term to facts. The Court is therefore likely to hold that substantial-evidence review applies to the BIA's persecution determination and affirm the First Circuit, possibly unanimously.

The Court has repeatedly insisted that the collateral-order doctrine stay 'narrow and selective' (Will, Mohawk, Digital Equipment), and Campbell-Ewald already said Yearsley protection is not absolute immunity. That points toward treating Yearsley as a defense to liability for authorized agents rather than a true immunity from suit, which makes a denial reviewable after final judgment. The Solicitor General's support for respondents on the jurisdictional question weakens GEO's claim that federal sovereign interests require immediate appeal. The fact-bound inquiry into what the government authorized, and whether GEO exceeded it, also overlaps with the merits, so the Court will likely affirm the Tenth Circuit's dismissal of GEO's appeal, probably unanimously or nearly so.

The Court's precedents in AFP v. Bonta and NAACP v. Alabama treat a compelled demand for donor identities as a present First Amendment burden, and the objectively reasonable chill it causes is an Article III injury. That injury does not depend on a later state-court enforcement order. Lexmark, Susan B. Anthony List, and the 'virtually unflagging' obligation to exercise jurisdiction make the Third Circuit's prudential-ripeness reasoning vulnerable, especially since forcing litigation into the state enforcement action risks res judicata stripping the federal forum (as in Smith & Wesson). A majority, likely including some liberal justices wary of subpoenas aimed at ideologically disfavored groups, will reverse and hold the first-filed § 1983 claim justiciable, with perhaps one dissent stressing the subpoena's non-self-executing nature.

The text of Rule 60(c)(1) plainly applies the 'reasonable time' requirement to every motion under Rule 60(b), including (b)(4), and Kemp already described the requirement as reaching all Rule 60(b) motions. The Court is likely to accept the Trustee's distinction between whether a judgment is void and the procedural rules for seeking relief from it in a particular motion; a timing rule does not make a void judgment valid, and other avenues such as collateral attack may remain. Klapprott and Espinosa did not decide the question, and the lower courts' atextual 'void means always reasonable' gloss is unlikely to persuade a textualist majority. The Court will likely affirm the Sixth Circuit, perhaps with a concurrence noting that what counts as a reasonable time may be lenient for void judgments, or that other remedies remain available.

The Court's recent ATS decisions (Jesner, Nestlé) and its broader hostility to judicially implied causes of action (Egbert v. Boule) strongly favor deferring to Congress, and Central Bank's presumption against civil aiding-and-abetting liability provides a ready doctrinal hook. The United States' support for petitioners, citing foreign-policy concerns about U.S. courts judging China's conduct on its own territory, reinforces Sosa step-two caution. On the TVPA, the text reaches only individuals who 'subject' another to torture, and Mohamad v. Palestinian Authority shows the Court reads that statute's liability provisions narrowly. The liberal Justices may dissent, particularly on the TVPA question given its Convention Against Torture background, but a conservative majority is likely to reverse the Ninth Circuit.

Section 1446(b)(1) is a deadline for a defendant's one-time choice of forum, not a statute of limitations for bringing a claim, so the Court is likely to hold that the Irwin presumption either does not apply (per Lozano) or is rebutted. The mandatory text, Congress's specific exceptions in §§ 1446(b)(3) and (c)(1), and the rule that removal statutes are strictly construed out of respect for state courts (Shamrock Oil) all cut against reading in an unwritten equitable exception. The facts are also unattractive for Enbridge: it removed about 887 days late, only after an adverse state-court ruling, raised the tolling theory for the first time on the merits, and could not show diligence or an extraordinary circumstance. Even justices open to equitable tolling in principle would likely affirm on these facts, leaving at most a lone dissent or concurrence that writes separately on the presumption.

The Irwin presumption of equitable tolling is aimed at limitations periods that govern when a claim may be brought. Section 1446(b)(1) is instead a forum-allocation deadline for defendants embedded in a detailed scheme, and § 1446(b)(3), § 1446(c)(1)'s bad-faith exception and other enumerated exceptions signal that Congress spelled out the permissible flexibility. The current Court's textualism (Rotkiske, Nutraceutical, Lozano) and federalism concerns about state-court authority point toward enforcing the 30-day deadline as written. Even if equity were available, Enbridge's deliberate 2.5 years of state-court litigation with full knowledge of its federal defenses would fail the diligence and extraordinary-circumstances test, giving the Court an easy alternative path to affirm.

Rule 60(c)(1) plainly says that any 'motion under Rule 60(b)' must be made within a reasonable time, and it singles out (b)(1)-(3) for an extra one-year cap, which leaves no textual room for a (b)(4) exception. Kemp's statement that all Rule 60(b) motions are subject to the reasonable-time requirement, together with drafting history showing the committee rejected a no-time-limit proposal, should reinforce a textualist majority. Petitioner's argument that a void judgment is a nullity confuses the status of a judgment with the procedural vehicle for vacating it; other avenues, such as collateral attack or an independent action, may remain. Klapprott and Espinosa did not decide the timing question, so the Court is likely to affirm the Sixth Circuit, probably unanimously or nearly so.

The current Court has steadily narrowed the ATS in Kiobel, Jesner, and Nestlé, and several Justices (Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, likely Kavanaugh and Barrett) are skeptical of any judicially created ATS cause of action beyond the three historical paradigms. Central Bank's presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting liability, together with the Solicitor General's support for petitioners on foreign-relations grounds, makes it likely the Court will hold that courts should not extend ATS liability to aiders and abettors. On the TVPA, the 'subjects an individual to torture' text and Mohamad's strict textualism point toward limiting liability to direct perpetrators and those with command responsibility. The liberal Justices may dissent, at least on the TVPA question, but a majority will likely reverse the Ninth Circuit.

The Court granted review of a closely divided Fifth Circuit ruling (7-6 en banc denial) that the United States opposes, and the Court has consistently read 'relating to' as requiring only a connection or association rather than a causal link or an explicit contractual directive. The textualist majority is likely to hold that the 2011 amendment rejects any contract-specific causal-nexus test. On that view, wartime crude production feeding federally contracted avgas refining, under pervasive Petroleum Administration for War control, is sufficiently related to acts under federal office to support removal, since a federal forum decides only where the case is heard, not the merits. The liberal justices may dissent on federalism grounds and on the need for limiting principles (Maracich, Dan's City), or the Court may vacate and remand under a clarified standard rather than order outright removal.

The Court's textualist majority is likely to view treating §403's nonretroactive anti-stacking amendment as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' as an end-run around Congress's express retroactivity choice in §403(b). It is also likely to reject the view that the ordinary operation of a prospective-only change in law is 'extraordinary.' After Loper Bright, the Court will police the outer bounds of the Commission's §994(t) delegation rather than defer, and will likely find that §1B1.13(b)(6) exceeds those bounds as applied to nonretroactive changes. The liberal justices, and possibly Gorsuch, may dissent, stressing the broad delegation, the single rehabilitation-only exclusion, and Concepcion's emphasis on judicial discretion to consider changes in law.

The Court granted certiorari after the Solicitor General recommended review and now supports Hikma, which strongly signals reversal. The Court's inducement precedents (Grokster, Global-Tech, Taamneh) require culpable, affirmative encouragement rather than accurate, routine statements made with knowledge that some downstream infringement will occur. Treating truthful statements that a product is a 'generic version' or AB-rated, plus citations of public sales figures, as plausible inducement would gut the section viii pathway Congress created and that Caraco recognized. The Court will likely hold that the complaint failed to plausibly allege active inducement, while leaving open liability for genuine off-label promotion of the patented use, with perhaps a couple of Justices dissenting on fact-bound pleading grounds.

The Court granted review over a fact-bound pleading objection, with the Solicitor General supporting Hikma, which signals that it intends to correct the Federal Circuit's expansive skinny-label inducement doctrine. Grokster, Global-Tech, and especially Twitter v. Taamneh call for culpable, affirmative conduct aimed at encouraging infringement, and calling a product a 'generic version,' noting its AB rating, or citing the brand's total sales is truthful, routine, and largely regulatory-driven. Letting such allegations survive dismissal would effectively nullify the section viii carve-out pathway Congress created, a structural argument the Court is likely to find persuasive. The Court will likely reverse, holding the complaint fails to plausibly allege active inducement, though a justice or two might stress the case-specific nature of the ruling or dissent.

A majority is likely to read 'extraordinary and compelling' as words of limitation that refer to individualized circumstances, not to a change in law that applies uniformly to everyone sentenced before the First Step Act. On that reading, using the general compassionate-release provision to apply § 403's amendment to final sentences would override Congress's specific nonretroactivity choice in § 403(b), especially since Congress made other provisions of the same Act (§ 404) expressly retroactive. Under § 994(a), the Commission's delegated power cannot produce a policy statement inconsistent with federal statutes, and after Loper Bright the Court will itself decide the statute's outer bounds, so § 1B1.13(b)(6) likely falls as applied here. Gorsuch or Roberts could join the Hewitt-style coalition, but the liberal justices are more likely to dissent, stressing the express delegation and Concepcion.

The Court granted review over a Fifth Circuit decision that appears to read the 2011 'relating to' amendment narrowly, and the Solicitor General supports the oil companies; both factors historically favor reversal. A majority is likely to hold that the amended statute requires only a connection or association between the challenged conduct and acts taken under federal direction. On that view, the government's allocation of crude from these designated 'critical fields' to petitioners' avgas refineries makes production sufficiently related to the federally directed refining. Federalism concerns and the risk of a limitless 'relating to' standard may draw dissents from the liberal justices, who could argue that the contracts never addressed production and that Watson bars treating regulated industry participation as 'acting under.'

In New Prime, Saxon, and Bissonnette the Court read § 1 by its 1925 ordinary meaning and rejected employer-friendly narrowing glosses, often unanimously. The pre-1925 FELA and Commerce Clause cases strongly support treating the intrastate final leg of a continuous interstate shipment as part of 'interstate commerce.' Saxon's focus on workers 'directly involved in transporting goods across borders' can therefore be read to include those carrying goods on the last segment of that journey. However, Flowers' argument that the journey ends at the warehouse, its workability concerns, and the cert grant on the employer's petition make a reversal quite plausible, so the prediction leans only modestly toward Brock.

The statute's text ties liability to trafficking in property that 'was confiscated' and to a plaintiff who 'owns the claim' to that property. Neither element contains the counterfactual temporal limit the Eleventh Circuit read in, and a textualist majority is likely to find Judge Brasher's dissent persuasive. The United States' support for petitioner on foreign-policy grounds, and the risk that the lower court's rule would gut Title III for leasehold and concession claimants, add further weight. Some Justices may be moved by the windfall and fairness concerns about Executive-authorized travel, so a likely outcome is reversal with a remand on the lawful-travel exclusion and damages, possibly over a dissent.

Saxon and Bissonnette both stressed that § 1 covers workers who play a 'direct and necessary role in the free flow of goods across borders,' and they focused on the worker's own work rather than the goods' journey. That framing gives the Court a path to hold that a purely intrastate distributor who buys goods at an in-state warehouse, after interstate haulers have unloaded them, is not engaged in interstate transportation. Respondent's 1925-era FELA and continuous-journey evidence is substantial, and the Court has sided with workers in New Prime, Saxon, and Bissonnette, so this is close. Still, concern about sweeping vast numbers of local delivery workers outside the FAA, plus the Court's narrow-construction mandate from Circuit City, slightly favors reversal of the Tenth Circuit.

The statute's text ties liability to whether the plaintiff currently 'owns the claim' to property that 'was confiscated' and whether the defendant 'traffics in' that property. Nothing in it calls for the Eleventh Circuit's counterfactual inquiry into whether the plaintiff's interest would have survived to the time of trafficking. The express inclusion of leasehold, future, and contingent interests in the definition of 'property', together with damages keyed to the certified claim value, reinforces petitioner's reading. The Solicitor General's support and the foreign-policy deterrence rationale should also weigh in petitioner's favor. Some justices may be moved by the windfall and fair-notice concerns about government-encouraged travel and dissent, or the Court may remand on the lawful-travel exception.

The current Court has repeatedly insisted that preemption be grounded in constitutional or statutory text rather than freewheeling judicial assessments of federal purposes (Virginia Uranium, Kansas v. Garcia, Rodriguez). That trend makes a broad, judge-made 'battlefield preemption' doctrine untethered from the FTCA's text vulnerable, particularly to Justices Thomas, Gorsuch, and likely Barrett, joining the three liberal Justices. The facts also help Hencely: the military found Fluor violated its contractual supervision duties, so imposing tort liability does not conflict with any federal directive, even under Boyle's own logic. Justices Kavanaugh (who joined Saleh on the D.C. Circuit) and Alito, and possibly the Chief, may side with Fluor and the Solicitor General on structural war-powers grounds, but a narrow holding for petitioner, limited to cases where the contractor violated military directives, seems more likely.

The Court's textualist turn in preemption doctrine (Virginia Uranium, Kansas v. Garcia) makes several justices, likely Thomas and Gorsuch, wary of extending Boyle's judge-made 'uniquely federal interests' displacement into a broad battlefield preemption that no statute directs. Section 2680(j) by its terms preserves only the United States' immunity, and the FTCA expressly excludes contractors from its definition of 'federal agency.' Even under Boyle and Campbell-Ewald, a contractor that allegedly violated the military's own instructions faces no 'significant conflict' between state duties and federal directives, so a narrow ruling reversing the Fourth Circuit is plausible. The Solicitor General's support for Fluor and the war-powers and military-discipline concerns will likely draw Alito, Kavanaugh, and possibly Roberts toward affirmance, making the outcome close.

This is a cert-stage petition from a Louisiana intermediate appellate court, and the Court is very unlikely to take it up. Title III of the ADA offers private plaintiffs no damages, and Cummings bars emotional-distress damages under § 504, so the federal question is likely not outcome-determinative for Doe's damages claims. The lower court also found the preemption argument conclusory and unsupported, which raises preservation problems, and the judgment rests heavily on a state-law determination about gross negligence. Even if the Court reached the merits, Felder and Haywood would favor Doe in principle, but the remedial limits and vehicle defects make denial or affirmance the most likely outcome.

This is a pro-style certiorari petition from a state intermediate appellate court, and it has serious vehicle defects. Title III of the ADA allows private plaintiffs no damages, and under Cummings emotional-distress damages are unavailable under § 504, so resolving the preemption question would likely not change the outcome. The state court also found the preemption argument conclusory and undeveloped, and the asserted split concerns state-law construction of COVID-immunity statutes rather than a federal question. The Court is very likely to deny certiorari, leaving the judgment for respondents intact.

A majority building on Carpenter (Roberts, Sotomayor, Kagan, Jackson), plus Gorsuch on a property/positive-law theory and likely Kavanaugh or Barrett, will probably hold that compelling Google to search users' stored Location History is a Fourth Amendment search, rejecting the government's third-party-doctrine argument. The Court is unlikely to adopt the Fifth Circuit's categorical rule that geofence warrants are inherently general warrants. Instead it will likely rule narrowly that this warrant's multi-step process was deficient, because it let officers expand the data and unmask users without further judicial authorization, leaving too much discretion to the executing officers. Remedy and good-faith questions would likely be remanded, so the judgment is vacated rather than the conviction definitively overturned, with Thomas, Alito and possibly another justice dissenting on third-party-doctrine grounds.

The Court's stays in Wilcox, Boyle, and this very case, together with the narrowing of Humphrey's Executor in Seila Law, signal that a six-Justice majority views removal protections for principal officers wielding substantial executive power as inconsistent with Article II. The majority will likely hold that the modern FTC exercises substantial executive power, whether by formally overruling Humphrey's Executor or by confining it to its 1935 conception. The Court may also limit courts' power to reinstate removed principal officers, though it could decline to reach that remedial question. The three liberal Justices will dissent, emphasizing stare decisis, the statutory text, and Congress's long-recognized authority to create independent multimember commissions, while the majority may carve out the Federal Reserve as distinct.

A majority will likely agree that querying Google's stored Location History is a Fourth Amendment search, drawing on Carpenter's rationale and Gorsuch-style property and positive-law theories, which narrows or rejects the panel's third-party-doctrine holding. However, the Court is unlikely to declare geofence warrants categorically unconstitutional general warrants, as the Fifth Circuit did. A warrant confined to a small area and a short time window, issued on probable cause that a crime occurred there, can plausibly satisfy probable cause and particularity, though the later expansion and deanonymization steps taken without returning to a magistrate are a real vulnerability. Given that, plus the backdrop of Leon good-faith reliance on a magistrate's warrant in an unsettled area, the most likely result is a closely divided affirmance that leaves Chatrie's conviction intact while setting some limits on future geofence warrants.

Heck's 'necessarily imply' test, read alongside Wilkinson v. Dotson and Wooley v. Maynard, most naturally leaves room for § 1983 suits seeking only prospective relief against future enforcement, because such relief does not undo or nullify a past conviction. Justices across the ideological spectrum are likely to resist a rule that lets a minor, uncustodial conviction permanently insulate a speech restriction from federal challenge by the very person most affected. The Court will probably rule narrowly that Heck does not bar purely prospective claims and leave the City's vehicle arguments (forfeiture, res judicata, the overlap with Siders) for remand. It may also avoid deciding the separate question of whether Heck applies to people who were never in custody.

Heck's favorable-termination rule targets § 1983 claims whose success would necessarily invalidate an existing conviction or sentence. An injunction against future enforcement of the ordinance neither vacates nor shortens Olivier's past penalty, so it falls on the permissible side of the line drawn in Wilkinson v. Dotson, Edwards v. Balisok, and Heck itself. The Fifth Circuit's rule would give previously convicted speakers less ability to challenge a law than never-prosecuted ones, which conflicts with Steffel and Wooley and is likely to trouble Justices across the ideological spectrum. The Court will probably decide narrowly on the prospective-relief question, avoid the broader habeas-access issue, and remand for consideration of the City's forfeiture and preclusion arguments.

The Court's trajectory in Seila Law, Collins, and Free Enterprise Fund, together with its stay orders in Wilcox and Boyle signaling that the government is likely to prevail on removal of officers wielding significant executive power, points strongly toward holding the FTC's removal protections unconstitutional as applied to today's Commission. The six conservative justices will likely either formally overrule Humphrey's Executor or confine it so narrowly that it no longer protects the modern FTC, which exercises substantial executive enforcement, rulemaking, and litigation power. The majority may avoid or narrowly address the remedial question about reinstatement, though some justices (e.g., Gorsuch, Thomas) would also hold courts lack power to reinstate removed principal officers. The three liberal justices will dissent, emphasizing stare decisis and congressional design of independent multimember agencies, possibly with the Federal Reserve carve-out noted by the majority.

The Court has repeatedly stressed that Rooker-Feldman is an exceptionally narrow doctrine confined to the circumstances of Rooker and Feldman. Exxon Mobil expressly described those circumstances as cases brought 'after the state proceedings ended.' Because the doctrine rests on the negative implication of § 1257, which reaches only final judgments of a state's highest court, it fits poorly with a trial-court consent order still on appeal; overlapping litigation is better handled by preclusion, abstention, and comity. The Court will likely reverse the Fourth Circuit, perhaps leaving respondents' concerns about forum-shopping and consent-order appealability for remand under those other doctrines.

Since Exxon Mobil, the Court has consistently and often unanimously confined Rooker-Feldman to its narrow origins (Exxon, Lance, Skinner), and it repeatedly warns lower courts against stretching it beyond cases where the state proceedings have ended. The doctrine rests on a negative inference from § 1257, which reaches only final judgments of a state's highest court. That textual tie, apparently supported by the United States as amicus, strongly suggests the doctrine cannot bar jurisdiction while a state appeal is still pending. The Court is likely to hold that parallel litigation is properly handled through preclusion, comity, and abstention doctrines rather than a jurisdictional bar, and to reverse the Fourth Circuit, perhaps remanding for consideration of those alternative grounds.

Wong Kim Ark's reasoning expressly adopted the English common-law jus soli rule, with narrow exceptions for diplomats' children, hostile occupiers and tribal Indians. Over 125 years of consistent executive, congressional and judicial practice, including the independent 1940/1952 statutory codification in § 1401(a), make the Government's 'complete political allegiance' reading very hard to sustain. Several conservative justices (Roberts, Kavanaugh, Barrett, Gorsuch) are likely to rest on text, history and precedent, possibly with the statutory ground offering an easier path. Thomas and Alito may dissent or concur only in part, perhaps distinguishing temporarily present or unlawfully present parents.

Wong Kim Ark's reasoning ties 'subject to the jurisdiction' to the common-law rule of jus soli, with only narrow exceptions: children of diplomats, children of hostile occupying forces, and tribal Indians. That reasoning readily covers children of unlawfully and temporarily present aliens, who are plainly bound by U.S. law. Even justices open to originalist reexamination will likely find the government's 'complete allegiance/domicile' theory historically thin. They will also see an independent statutory ground in 8 U.S.C. § 1401(a), codified in 1940 and 1952 against a settled understanding, which counsels against upending more than a century of practice by executive order. I expect a majority of the Chief Justice, Kavanaugh, Barrett, Gorsuch and the three liberals, with Thomas and possibly Alito dissenting or concurring only on narrower grounds.

The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the LPR 'has committed' a covered offense, which is a historical fact fixed at the time of reentry. Nothing in the statute limits the evidence used to prove that fact in later removal proceedings to what the government held at the border. The deferred-inspection and parole framework presupposes that facts will be developed after entry, and the Second Circuit's rule would make parole largely useless whenever charges are pending. The Court granted the Solicitor General's petition and is likely to reverse with a textualist majority, perhaps with a narrow dissent stressing LPR protections and the Fleuti/Vartelas tradition.

Unlike the SEC scheme in Jarkesy, an FCC forfeiture order is not a self-executing judgment. No penalty can be collected unless the government sues in district court, where the carrier gets a de novo jury trial, and § 504(c) limits any prejudicial use of unpaid forfeitures. A majority is therefore likely to hold that the jury right is preserved and that a carrier which pays and seeks § 402 review has waived it. Justices Gorsuch, Thomas, and possibly Alito may accept the carriers' argument that the practical coercion of defying a federal penalty order makes the jury right illusory, but most of the Court is unlikely to extend Jarkesy this far.

The current Court's textualist majority is likely to read 'arrives in the United States' according to its ordinary meaning, which requires physical entry onto U.S. soil, and to treat 'physically present in' and 'arrives in' as covering different temporal and procedural situations rather than finding surplusage. Sale v. Haitian Centers Council and the presumption against extraterritoriality bolster the reading that INA duties do not extend to aliens still in Mexico. The Court also tends to defer to executive border-management discretion and to construe § 706(1) narrowly under Norton v. SUWA, which requires a discrete, mandatory duty. The three liberal justices would likely dissent, stressing the anti-circumvention concern and the surplusage argument; mootness or rescission concerns could produce a vacatur instead of a merits ruling, but a reversal is most probable.

Jarkesy's six-justice majority held that punitive civil penalties resembling common-law claims are 'Suits at common law' that Congress cannot route around a jury, and the government's position appears to concede the penalties are legal in nature. That leaves the decisive question whether the § 504 de novo collection suit cures the problem. The government has a real argument that an FCC order is not self-executing and a jury remains available, which could attract Roberts or Barrett. Still, the practical burdens are significant: the order has collateral consequences, a carrier must pay to get prompt appellate review, and the government controls whether and when to sue. Those features will likely persuade the Jarkesy majority that the jury right is illusory in practice, though the outcome is close.

The Court's textualist majority is likely to read 'arrives in the United States' as requiring physical presence on U.S. soil, reinforced by the presumption against extraterritoriality and by Sale v. Haitian Centers Council's refusal to extend INA protections to aliens outside U.S. territory. Respondents' surplusage argument has some force, but it is weakened because 'arrives in' can sensibly cover those just crossing at ports of entry or arriving by sea or air, as distinct from those already physically present. The government's border-management and foreign-affairs authority, together with Thuraissigiam's limits on threshold rights, gives the conservative justices further reasons to reverse the Ninth Circuit. The liberal justices will likely dissent, stressing the perverse incentive to cross unlawfully and the fact that the officers' conduct was domestic, though the policy's rescission creates some chance of a mootness-based disposition.

The text of § 1101(a)(13)(C)(v) turns on whether the LPR 'has committed' an offense, which is a historical fact, not on what border officers could prove at reentry. Nothing in the INA confines the government's proof in removal proceedings to evidence it held on the day of reentry. Lau was paroled for deferred inspection and so remained an arriving alien, and his later conviction conclusively shows he committed the offense before he returned. The Vartelas footnote and the concern for LPR protections may draw dissents from the more liberal justices, but a textualist majority is likely to reverse the Second Circuit and leave the moral-turpitude question for remand.

Traditional equitable disgorgement and accounting for profits, as reflected in the Restatement (Third) of Restitution § 51, are measured by the wrongdoer's unjust gain rather than the claimant's loss. That makes a pecuniary-harm prerequisite hard to square with the remedy's historical scope. Liu's 'for victims' language most naturally addresses where disgorged funds go and bars a pure windfall to the Treasury, not whether investors must prove a monetary loss before profits can be stripped. The 2021 amendments in §§ 78u(d)(3) and (d)(7) give an independent textual basis for disgorgement with no loss requirement, though justices skeptical of SEC power (likely Thomas, Gorsuch, and perhaps one other) may side with petitioner on Kokesh/Liu penalty-avoidance grounds.

The petition seeks summary reversal of a divided Fourth Circuit panel that granted habeas relief after faulting the state court's opinion for lacking 'nuance' and 'exhaustiveness.' This Court has repeatedly and summarily reversed such grants, holding that AEDPA deference attaches to the state court's decision rather than the thoroughness of its reasoning (Richter, Visciotti, Woods v. Donald). Here the state court recited the correct Kyles standard, and Strickler permits weighing the strength of the other evidence, so fairminded jurists could disagree about materiality. The likeliest outcome is a per curiam reversal, possibly with dissents from Justices Sotomayor and/or Jackson stressing that the case is fact-bound and that the state court effectively applied a sufficiency-of-the-evidence test.
