Traditional equitable accounting for profits, as reflected in the Restatement (Third) of Restitution and the trust and intellectual-property cases Liu relied on, measured relief by the wrongdoer's gain and did not require the plaintiff to prove a loss. That history supports the Ninth Circuit's reading that Liu's 'for victims' language governs how the money is used, not whether it can be ordered. Congress's 2021 express authorization of 'disgorgement' in §§ 78u(d)(3) and (d)(7) gives the government an additional textual basis, and the Court may be reluctant to let fraudsters keep profits merely because investor losses are hard to prove. Still, this Court's recent skepticism of SEC remedial power (Kokesh, Jarkesy, AMG) could produce a narrower ruling or votes from Justices such as Gorsuch and Thomas for the petitioner, so a reversal is a real possibility.

The State seeks summary reversal, a posture this Court has repeatedly used against circuits (often the Fourth, Sixth and Ninth) that grant habeas relief without the deference Harrington v. Richter requires. The Fourth Circuit conceded that the state court correctly stated the Kyles standard, yet faulted it for an insufficiently 'nuanced' and 'exhaustive' analysis; this resembles the error the Court corrected in cases like Woods v. Donald and Bell v. Cone, because AEDPA deference attaches to the state court's decision, not the thoroughness of its opinion. Weighing the strength of the remaining, unimpeached evidence is permissible under Strickler, so fairminded jurists could disagree about materiality, which bars relief. The liberal justices (likely Sotomayor and/or Jackson) may dissent or say they would deny the petition, since the case is fact-bound and the Fourth Circuit's sufficiency-of-the-evidence critique has some force.

Under Cabrales and Rodriguez-Moreno, venue turns on where the essential conduct elements occurred. Section 1519's only conduct element is falsifying the record, which happened entirely in Seattle; the intent to obstruct is a mental state, and neither transmission nor actual obstruction is required. A textualist majority, with Justice Gorsuch's strong interest in vicinage protections, is likely to reject an effects-based theory that would let prosecutors choose broadly among forums, in tension with Travis. Some Justices may find the Government's historical point persuasive, that obstruction offenses have traditionally been tried where the obstructed proceeding sits, along with its argument that sending the invoice to the San Francisco office was part of the offense, so a divided Court is plausible.

The Court's venue precedents (Cabrales, Rodriguez-Moreno, Travis, Johnston) tie the locus delicti to the essential conduct elements, and § 1519's only conduct element, falsifying the record, was completed in Seattle; the intent-to-obstruct clause is a mens rea, not an act. Congress's enactment of a specific venue provision for §§ 1503 and 1512 (18 U.S.C. § 1512(i)), placing venue where the obstructed proceeding sits, strongly implies that no such effects-based venue exists for § 1519 absent statutory text. The government's fallback theory, that the email 'created' a copy of the record in N.D. Cal., is factually awkward because the agents received it while sitting in Seattle, and it is unlikely to command a majority. Justices across the spectrum have shown sympathy for founding-era venue and vicinage protections, though a couple of justices (e.g., Alito) may accept the inchoate-obstruction or effects rationale.

The Fourth Circuit majority granted relief on a Sixth Amendment impartial-jury and structural-error theory that Sweeney never pressed on appeal. That is a clear departure from the party-presentation principle reaffirmed in Sineneng-Smith and Greenlaw. The majority also bypassed exhaustion and never applied AEDPA's deferential standard to the one claim that was exhausted, which is the kind of habeas error this Court routinely corrects by summary per curiam reversal. The Court is likely to summarily reverse on party-presentation grounds and remand, probably without noted dissent, though a liberal justice could dissent from summary disposition.

The Fourth Circuit majority granted relief on impartial-jury and structural-error theories that Sweeney never pressed, which closely tracks the departure from party presentation the Court condemned in Sineneng-Smith. The majority also never applied AEDPA's deferential standard to the one exhausted claim. No Supreme Court holding clearly establishes that Remmer extends to a juror's crime-scene visit, and Greer v. United States limits structural error, so the panel's reasoning is vulnerable on several independent grounds. The Court has a history of summarily reversing circuits that disregard AEDPA, so it is likely to issue a per curiam summary reversal, at least on party-presentation grounds, with few or no noted dissents.

In Wilcox the Court went out of its way to call the Federal Reserve a uniquely structured, quasi-private entity, and the government here concedes the for-cause protection is constitutional, so the case turns on whether the President's cause determination is effectively unreviewable. That position would make the protection meaningless. Justices like Kavanaugh and Barrett have signaled concern about Fed independence and about letting a removal take effect before any process or judicial review, which makes keeping the status quo during litigation the more likely course. A majority will probably deny the stay, perhaps on narrow grounds such as inadequate notice and opportunity to respond or the balance of equities, while Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch dissent in favor of broad presidential removal discretion and limits on reinstatement remedies.

New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as a flexible equitable doctrine that does not punish inadvertence or mistake, and the Fifth Circuit's knowledge-plus-motive rule effectively presumes bad faith, since a Chapter 13 debtor almost always knows of his claim and almost always has a motive to conceal it. The United States supports vacatur, and the majority of circuits use a holistic inquiry, so the Court is likely to vacate and remand with instructions to weigh all relevant evidence of intent. It may stop short of requiring a free-standing subjective bad-faith finding and may emphasize objective indicia, which would let the respondent still prevail on remand. Some justices might accept the respondent's argument that the inference is merely permissible circumstantial proof, but the outcome most likely favors the petitioner by a wide margin.

Having unanimously held in Tyler that the government may not keep more than it is owed, the Court likely granted review to correct the Sixth Circuit's rule that a government-run forced-sale price conclusively fixes just compensation, especially on facts showing a sale at roughly 40% of market value. A majority will probably hold that just compensation is measured by the value of the equity taken, so the auction price is relevant evidence but not automatically dispositive, while leaving room for properly conducted, commercially reasonable sales. Several Justices may side with the county, citing the historical surplus-proceeds tradition, BFP's distinction between forced-sale and market value, and administrability concerns. The Court will likely decline to reach or reject the Excessive Fines question.

The Court granted review of a clear circuit split, and the United States supports vacatur. New Hampshire v. Maine's framing of judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine aimed at deliberate manipulation sits uneasily with a rule that infers bad faith from knowledge plus a motive that nearly every Chapter 13 debtor has. The Court's skepticism of judge-made equitable doctrines that override the Bankruptcy Code's calibrated remedies (Law v. Siegel) points the same way, as does the windfall the Fifth Circuit's rule gives tortfeasors at creditors' expense. The likely outcome is vacatur and remand for a holistic, all-circumstances inquiry, though some Justices may note that the lower court's alternative application of the Slater factors suggests the same result on remand, and a dissent or concurrence could stress trial-court discretion.

In Trump v. Wilcox the Court already signaled that the Federal Reserve is a 'uniquely structured, quasi-private entity' whose removal protections stand apart from the broader unitary-executive project. Here the government expressly disclaims any constitutional challenge, leaving a statutory 'for cause' question on which the President's reading (essentially unreviewable cause based on unadjudicated, pre-tenure private conduct, with no notice or hearing) would hollow out the protection Congress adopted in 1935. Pivotal justices such as Kavanaugh, Barrett and the Chief Justice are likely to worry about Fed independence, market stability, and the procedural irregularity of removal without any meaningful chance to respond. That makes a denial of the stay, leaving Cook in office pending litigation, the more likely outcome, with Thomas, Alito and Gorsuch likely dissenting on executive-power and remedial grounds.

Badgerow addressed freestanding §§ 9–10 applications filed as new proceedings. Here the district court's original federal-question jurisdiction over a live case never lapsed during the § 3 stay, and Smith v. Spizzirri stressed that a stay, rather than dismissal, keeps the federal court available to finish the dispute after arbitration. A majority is likely to treat a motion to confirm filed in the same pending action as within the court's existing jurisdiction, or alternatively within § 1367(a) supplemental jurisdiction, reasoning that the award resolves the very claims the court already had before it. Some textualist justices may agree with petitioner that Badgerow's face-of-the-application rule governs every §§ 9–10 application, but forcing the parties into state court mid-case seems inefficient and anomalous to most of the Court.

Under Michigan's scheme, the county takes absolute title to the whole home at foreclosure, before any sale. Tyler's logic and the traditional just-compensation measure (Miller, Olson, 564.54 Acres) therefore point toward fair market value at the time of the taking, less the debt, rather than whatever a depressed auction happens to yield. The Court's decision to grant review of a Sixth Circuit bright-line rule suggests some appetite to correct it, and the property-rights coalition from Tyler may hold, possibly with a narrow holding that the auction price is not conclusive and a remand. However, Nelson, historical tax-sale practice, BFP's respect for forced-sale prices, and serious administrability concerns make a respondent win quite plausible, and the Court will likely avoid the Excessive Fines question entirely.

Badgerow involved freestanding §§ 9/10 applications filed as new actions. Here the district court already had original federal-question jurisdiction over a pending case that § 3 and Spizzirri required it to stay rather than dismiss. Spizzirri itself said keeping the case on the docket lets the court help the arbitration and later facilitate recovery on the award, so the Court will likely treat confirmation or vacatur motions as part of the same case or controversy, whether through retained jurisdiction or § 1367(a). Some textualist justices may accept the petitioner's (and apparently the government's) view that Badgerow's application-face rule applies regardless of an anchor case, so a modest dissent is plausible.
